items.q: What is the author's central contention regarding the Court's authority?
o: The Rome Statute enjoys universal acceptance among all states.
The Court's authority is fundamentally constrained by its dependence on jurisdiction claims and cooperation that not all states accept.
Territorial jurisdiction has been abandoned by the Court in favour of nationality-based jurisdiction.
Arrest warrants against heads of state are always executed by states parties.
items.e: Kernthese im ersten Absatz: „the Court's writ runs only as far as states allow it to“ — die Autorität hängt von Zustimmung und Kooperation ab, die nicht alle Staaten leisten.
items.passage:
The International Criminal Court was conceived, in the optimistic afterglow of Rome in 1998, as the capstone of a slowly cohering system of international justice — the tribunal to which no perpetrator of the gravest crimes would ultimately be beyond reach. A quarter of a century on, that ambition sits awkwardly beside a starker reality: the Court's writ runs only as far as states allow it to, and jurisdiction, far from being a settled foundation, has become the terrain on which its legitimacy is fought over case by case.

The difficulty is structural rather than incidental. The Rome Statute binds only its parties, yet the Court has repeatedly asserted authority over nationals of non-member states where the alleged conduct occurred on the territory of a member, a reading that Washington, Moscow and Beijing alike have denounced as an unwarranted extension of treaty law to those who never consented to it. Prosecutors counter that territorial competence has always attached to the place of the crime, not the nationality of the accused, and that any other rule would let non-parties export impunity across their borders simply by dispatching nationals to commit it. Both positions are coherent; neither commands universal assent, and that absence of assent is precisely the point.

Arrest warrants issued against sitting heads of state have sharpened the quarrel further. States parties owe a treaty obligation to execute them, yet several have declined to do so when the wanted official arrived on a diplomatic visit, pleading competing obligations under customary immunity or simple political prudence. The Court has no marshals of its own; it depends entirely on the goodwill of governments it cannot compel, and each unexecuted warrant erodes the presumption that its rulings carry consequence rather than merely rhetorical weight.

None of this renders the institution ornamental. Even an unenforced warrant narrows a fugitive's travel, and the mere existence of a permanent forum has altered the calculations of some belligerents. But an institution whose authority rests on voluntary compliance is, by definition, only ever as strong as the least cooperative of its members choose to make it — a truth the Court's founders acknowledged in private, whatever they proclaimed in Rome.
items.src: Übungstext im Stil von Foreign Affairs / The Economist (nicht offiziell)

items.q: According to the passage, on what basis does the Court assert authority over nationals of non-member states?
o: Because those states have signed a bilateral agreement with the Court.
Because the alleged conduct occurred on the territory of a member state.
Because the UN Security Council has referred every such case.
Because customary international law binds all states regardless of consent.
items.e: Textbeleg: „the Court has repeatedly asserted authority over nationals of non-member states where the alleged conduct occurred on the territory of a member.“

items.q: Which three states are named as denouncing this reading of jurisdiction?
o: France, Germany and the United Kingdom
items.e: Textbeleg: „Washington, Moscow and Beijing alike have denounced as an unwarranted extension of treaty law…“

items.q: What can be inferred about the Court's capacity to enforce its own arrest warrants?
o: It maintains an independent police force capable of arrests in any territory.
It relies entirely on the cooperation of national governments, which it cannot compel.
It only issues warrants once the accused has already surrendered voluntarily.
It has never issued a warrant against a sitting head of state.
items.e: Textbeleg: „The Court has no marshals of its own; it depends entirely on the goodwill of governments it cannot compel.“

items.q: In the final paragraph, 'ornamental' is used to mean that the institution would be …
o: merely decorative and without real effect.
items.e: „ornamental“ = rein schmückend, wirkungslos. Der Autor verneint dies zwar („None of this renders…“), die Wortbedeutung selbst bleibt aber „wirkungslos/dekorativ“.

items.q: The author's overall tone toward the ICC's predicament is best described as …
o: dismissive of the Court's relevance entirely.
sympathetic to the Court's founders while clear-eyed about its structural limits.
triumphalist about the Court's growing authority.
items.e: Der Ton erkennt reale Wirkung an („None of this renders the institution ornamental“), bleibt aber nüchtern-kritisch gegenüber den strukturellen Grenzen.

items.q: What is the primary function of the final paragraph?
o: To refute every argument made in the preceding paragraphs.
To qualify the preceding critique by acknowledging the Court's genuine, if limited, effect.
To introduce a wholly new topic unrelated to jurisdiction.
To announce that the Court will soon dissolve.
items.e: Konzessive Struktur „None of this renders… But an institution whose authority rests on…“ — Einschränkung der vorherigen Kritik, keine völlige Widerlegung.

items.q: Why do prosecutors defend the Court's approach to territorial jurisdiction?
o: Because nationality-based jurisdiction is easier to prove in court.
Because they argue jurisdiction has always attached to the place where the crime occurred.
Because the UN Charter requires it explicitly.
Because non-member states have consented to it informally.
items.e: Textbeleg: „territorial competence has always attached to the place of the crime, not the nationality of the accused.“

items.q: The prosecutor decided to ____ the former minister on three counts of crimes against humanity.
items.e: „to indict“ = förmlich anklagen. „impeach“ betrifft Amtsenthebungsverfahren, „implicate“ = verwickeln ohne formale Anklage.

items.q: The court unsealed the ____ only after the suspect had been taken into custody.
items.e: „to unseal an indictment“ ist eine feste US-rechtliche Kollokation; eine bloße „allegation“ wird nicht „versiegelt“.

items.q: The suspect will be ____ before a judge within 48 hours of arrest.
items.e: „to arraign“ = dem Haftrichter vorführen und die Anklage verlesen; zeitlich vor jeder Verurteilung.

items.q: At the ____, the defendant entered a plea of not guilty.
items.e: Beim „arraignment“ (Vorführungstermin) wird das Plädoyer abgegeben, nicht bei der bloßen „indictment“ (Anklageschrift).

items.q: Facing overwhelming evidence, the defendant accepted a plea ____ rather than risk trial.
items.e: Feste Kollokation „plea bargain“; „deal“ ist umgangssprachlich und keine Fachkollokation, „pact/accord“ passen nicht.

items.q: The jury chose to ____ the defendant on all charges.
items.e: „to acquit somebody on a charge“ ist die feste strafprozessuale Kollokation; „exonerate/absolve“ nehmen kein „on“-Objekt in dieser Form.

items.q: The ____ was met with outrage among victims' families.
items.e: „acquittal“ = Freispruch nach Verhandlung; „dismissal“ wäre eine Abweisung schon vor der Verhandlung.

items.q: It took the jury only two hours to ____ him of fraud.
items.e: „to convict somebody of“ = für schuldig befinden; „sentence“ folgt erst nach der Verurteilung.

items.q: His earlier ____ was overturned on appeal after new evidence emerged.
items.e: „conviction“ = das Schuldurteil selbst, das im Berufungsverfahren aufgehoben werden kann.

items.q: The suspect remains in ____ pending trial.
items.e: „to remain in custody“ ist die feste Fügung für Untersuchungshaft; „arrest“ bezeichnet den Akt der Festnahme selbst.

items.q: Police were authorised to ____ the diplomat's driver for questioning.
items.e: „detain“ = vorübergehend festhalten (schwächer als „arrest“); passt zur Kollokation „for questioning“.

items.q: The judge issued an arrest ____ naming the fugitive minister.
items.e: „arrest warrant“ = Haftbefehl; eine „summons“ lädt lediglich vor Gericht, ohne Festnahme anzuordnen.

items.q: He received a ____ ordering him to appear in court as a defendant.
items.e: „summons“ lädt eine Verfahrenspartei vor Gericht; „subpoena“ betrifft spezifisch Zeugen oder die Vorlage von Unterlagen.

items.q: The appellate court moved to ____ the indictment for lack of evidence.
items.e: „to quash an indictment“ ist die spezifische Kollokation; „overturn“ passt eher zu „verdict“, „vacate“ eher zu „sentence“.

items.q: On appeal, the higher court decided to ____ the jury's verdict.
items.e: „to overturn a verdict“ ist die Standardkollokation im Berufungsverfahren.

items.q: The Supreme Court chose to ____ the lower court's decision in full.
items.e: „to uphold a decision“ = bestätigen; das Gegenteil von „overturn“.

items.q: The judge agreed to ____ the sentence in light of the procedural error.
items.e: „to vacate a sentence“ = ein Strafmaß aufheben; feste Kollokation im US-amerikanischen Recht.

items.q: The judge ordered the defendant ____ in custody until trial.
items.e: „to remand somebody in custody“ ist der feste strafprozessuale Ausdruck; die anderen Verben passen nicht in diese exakte Fügung.

items.q: Three judges sat on the ____ for the appeal, while the defendant watched from the dock.
items.e: „the bench“ bezeichnet die Richterbank bzw. die Richter kollektiv; „the dock“ ist der Platz des Angeklagten.

items.q: The case was added to the court's crowded ____ for next term.
items.e: „docket“ (v. a. AE) = Terminkalender bzw. Liste anhängiger Fälle.

items.q: ____ persons before the Court retain the right to a fair and public hearing.
items.e: Die Terminologie des Gerichtshofs lautet „the accused“ — nicht „defendant“, ein Begriff nationaler Strafprozesse.

items.q: In domestic criminal trials, the ____ enjoys the presumption of innocence, just as the accused does before the Court.
items.e: „defendant“ ist das nationale Pendant zu „the accused“ vor dem IStGH; „claimant/plaintiff“ gehören zum Zivilprozess.

items.q: The panel was convened to ____ disputes over admissibility.
items.e: „adjudicate“ = richterlich entscheiden; „arbitrate“ gehört zum privaten Schiedsverfahren, „mediate“ zur unverbindlichen Vermittlung.

items.q: The tribunal found the commander ____ for failing to prevent the atrocity.
items.e: „culpable“ = strafrechtlich schuldhaft; „liable“ ist der zivilrechtliche Begriff für Haftung — die klassische Registerunterscheidung.

items.q: The victims' representatives were granted ____ to participate in the proceedings.
items.e: „to be granted standing“ = Klage-/Verfahrensbefugnis erhalten; „stance/stand“ sind klanglich nahe, aber falsche Distraktoren.

items.q: The registrar issued a ____ compelling the archivist to hand over the sealed correspondence.
items.e: „subpoena“ = gerichtliche Anordnung zur Vorlage von Unterlagen oder zum Erscheinen als Zeuge; „summons“ lädt lediglich eine Verfahrenspartei vor.

items.q: The prosecutor insisted that the witness ____ under oath.
items.e: Mandativer Subjunktiv nach „insist that“ — Grundform ohne -s.

items.q: It is essential that the accused ____ present at every hearing.
items.e: Mandativer Subjunktiv nach „it is essential that“ — bloße Grundform „be“.

items.q: Had the state ratified the Statute earlier, the Court ____ jurisdiction from the outset.
items.e: Typ-3-Konditionalsatz: irreale Vergangenheitsbedingung, Folge ebenfalls in der Vergangenheit.

items.q: If the warrant ____ issued last year, the suspect would already be in custody today.
items.e: Gemischter Konditionalsatz: Bedingung in der Vergangenheit, Folge in der Gegenwart („today“).

items.q: ____ the delegation to walk out, the negotiations would collapse entirely.
items.e: „Should… to walk out“; nach „Should“ folgt der bloße Infinitiv ohne „to“ — hier ausnahmsweise mit „to walk out“ als Konstruktionsmuster wie „Were… to“.

items.q: ____ the panel to dismiss every charge at the confirmation stage, years of investigation would count for nothing.
items.e: „Were… to dismiss“ = hypothetische, konditionale Inversion mit „to“-Infinitiv.

items.q: Little ____ that the arrest warrant would provoke such a diplomatic backlash.
items.e: Negative Inversion nach vorangestelltem „Little“: Hilfsverb vor Subjekt.

items.q: Under no circumstances ____ the tribunal disclose the identity of a protected witness.
items.e: Negative Inversion nach vorangestelltem „Under no circumstances“.

items.q: He told the investigators that he ____ never met the accused before that night.
items.e: Past Perfect nach Backshift in der indirekten Rede (Vorzeitigkeit zum Berichtszeitpunkt).

items.q: She said the hearing ____ take place the following week, not that week.
items.e: Backshift von „will“ zu „would“ in der indirekten Rede; „the following week“ statt „next week“ (Deixisverschiebung).

items.q: They ____ have received the summons; the registry never sent it.
items.e: „can't have“ = logische Unmöglichkeit im Rückblick.

items.q: The commander ____ have known about the massacre, given the volume of intercepted communications.
items.e: „must have“ = logische Gewissheit im Rückblick, gestützt durch den Beleg im Nebensatz.

items.q: ____ struck the observers most was the tribunal's restraint in sentencing.
items.e: Pseudo-Cleft-Satz: „What … was …“.

items.q: It was the absence of enforcement, not the absence of evidence, ____ ultimately doomed the case.
items.e: Es-Spaltsatz („It was … that …“) zur Hervorhebung.

items.q: The longer the warrant went unexecuted, ____ the Court's credibility appeared.
items.e: Korrelative Struktur „the … the …“; der zweite bestimmte Artikel ist obligatorisch.

items.q: The more governments ignore the warrants, ____ the deterrent effect becomes.
items.e: Korrelative Struktur „the … the …“ mit Komparativ im zweiten Satzglied.

items.q: No sooner had the warrant been issued ____ the minister cancelled his foreign trip.
items.e: Feste Korrelation „no sooner … than“; „then“ ist Adverb, kein Konnektor.

items.q: Hardly had the trial begun ____ the defence challenged the tribunal's jurisdiction.
items.e: Feste Korrelation „hardly … when“; nach vorangestelltem „Hardly“ steht die Inversion, danach „when“.

items.q: The minister is said ____ the file weeks before the leak became public.
items.e: Berichtspassiv mit Vorzeitigkeit: „is said to have seen“.

items.q: The former general is widely believed ____ the massacre from a nearby command post.
items.e: Berichtspassiv „is believed to have ordered“ drückt Vorzeitigkeit zum jetzigen Glauben aus.

items.q: ____ before the tribunal in 2019, the general has never again left his home country.
items.e: Passivisches Partizip: der General wurde angeklagt, er klagte nicht selbst an.

items.q: ____ its jurisdictional limits, the Court has still secured a number of convictions.
items.e: „notwithstanding“ + Nominalphrase (ohne „of“); „despite of“ ist falsch, „although“ verlangt einen Nebensatz.

items.q: He read the ruling and ____ at once.
items.e: Feste Rektion „appeal against a ruling“ (BE); das bloße transitive „appeal it“ ist eher AE-umgangssprachlich und hier nicht die gesuchte Form.

items.q: The prosecutor read the file and ____ before the hearing.
items.e: Pronominales Objekt „it“ ist nach transitivem „summarise“ obligatorisch.

items.q: A number of witnesses ____ still to be interviewed by investigators.
items.e: „a number of“ + Plural — im Gegensatz zu „the number of“ + Singular.

items.q: The tribunal has yet to rule ____ the admissibility of the intercepted communications.
items.e: Feste Rektion: „rule on“ = entscheiden über; „rule over“ = herrschen über.

items.q: Which statement best captures the author's overall argument?
o: The shift from absolute to restrictive immunity has produced a single, uniform global standard.
Despite the shift toward a restrictive doctrine, courts in different jurisdictions still draw the line between sovereign and commercial acts differently, generating persistent litigation.
Sovereign immunity has been abolished entirely in London, New York and Luxembourg.
Bondholders now enjoy no legal remedies whatsoever against defaulting states.
items.e: Kernthese im ersten Absatz: „the line between the two continues to be drawn differently in London, New York and Luxembourg, with predictably untidy results.“
items.passage:
Few doctrines of international law have proved as resistant to tidy codification as sovereign immunity, and few have generated as much recent litigation. The old absolute rule — that a state and its property were simply beyond the reach of a foreign court — has given way almost everywhere to a restrictive doctrine distinguishing sovereign acts from commercial ones, yet the line between the two continues to be drawn differently in London, New York and Luxembourg, with predictably untidy results for litigants who find themselves arguing the same facts before three benches at once.

Nowhere has the doctrine been tested more severely than in suits brought by bondholders against defaulting governments. A state that issues debt in New York under New York law has, courts have increasingly held, surrendered its protection for that transaction even where the underlying purpose of the borrowing was unmistakably sovereign; the commercial character of the instrument, not the use to which the proceeds were put, now governs the inquiry. Creditors have pressed the logic further still, seeking to attach embassy bank accounts and even satellites, only to run into a separate and more stubborn wall: protection from execution survives even where protection from suit has fallen, and courts have generally refused to treat the two as interchangeable.

The resulting asymmetry frustrates claimants and defendants in roughly equal measure. A plaintiff may win a resounding judgment and then discover that almost nothing the defendant state owns abroad is actually attachable, since diplomatic and central-bank assets enjoy a separate, more robust layer of protection that survives even a clear commercial waiver. Governments, for their part, complain that the erosion of absolute immunity has turned ordinary sovereign borrowing into a minefield of foreign litigation, discouraging exactly the market access that developing states most need. Neither side has much cause for satisfaction, and the doctrine, restrictive in name, remains anything but restrained in the courtroom disputes it continues to generate.
items.src: Übungstext im Stil von Foreign Affairs / The Economist (nicht offiziell)

items.q: According to the passage, what determines whether a state's bond issuance counts as a commercial act?
o: The nationality of the majority of bondholders.
The sovereign purpose for which the borrowed funds were ultimately used.
The commercial character of the instrument itself, regardless of the purpose of the borrowing.
Whether the bond was issued before or after the state joined the United Nations.
items.e: Textbeleg: „the commercial character of the instrument, not the use to which the proceeds were put, now governs the inquiry.“

items.q: What happens when creditors attempt to attach embassy bank accounts or satellites?
o: They routinely succeed, since any waiver of immunity from suit automatically extends to execution.
They run into a separate, more stubborn layer of protection that survives even where immunity from suit has fallen.
Such attempts are legally impossible and have therefore never been attempted.
They succeed only in Luxembourg, never in London or New York.
items.e: Textbeleg: „protection from execution survives even where protection from suit has fallen, and courts have generally refused to treat the two as interchangeable.“

items.q: What can be inferred about a plaintiff who wins a judgment against a defaulting state?
o: The plaintiff can be certain of recovering the full amount from any state asset abroad.
The plaintiff may find that diplomatic and central-bank assets remain shielded, leaving little that is actually attachable.
The plaintiff automatically forfeits the judgment if the state pleads sovereign immunity.
The plaintiff must first obtain permission from the state's own courts before enforcing abroad.
items.e: Textbeleg: „A plaintiff may win a resounding judgment and then discover that almost nothing the defendant state owns abroad is actually attachable.“

items.q: In the final paragraph, the word 'minefield' is used to convey that sovereign borrowing has become …
o: fraught with unpredictable legal risk from foreign litigation.
entirely prohibited under current treaty law.
cheaper than it was under the absolute immunity doctrine.
items.e: Metaphorisch: „turned ordinary sovereign borrowing into a minefield of foreign litigation“ = mit unkalkulierbaren rechtlichen Risiken behaftet.

items.q: The author's tone toward the current state of sovereign immunity doctrine is best described as …
o: triumphant about the clarity the restrictive doctrine has achieved.
dismissive of the entire body of case law as irrelevant.
analytical and somewhat wry, noting the doctrine is 'restrictive in name' but 'anything but restrained' in practice.
alarmist, predicting the imminent collapse of state borrowing markets.
items.e: Der Schlusssatz („restrictive in name, remains anything but restrained“) zeigt einen analytisch-ironischen, aber nicht alarmistischen Ton.

items.q: What role does the final paragraph play in the overall argument?
o: To introduce a wholly new legal doctrine unrelated to immunity.
To show that the asymmetry created by the restrictive doctrine leaves both plaintiffs and defendant states dissatisfied.
To argue that governments should return to the absolute immunity rule.
To summarise the history of the Rome Statute.
items.e: Der Absatz erklärt, warum „Neither side has much cause for satisfaction“ — die Asymmetrie trifft Kläger wie beklagte Staaten gleichermaßen.

items.q: Why, according to the passage, do litigants find themselves arguing similar facts before courts in different countries?
o: Because international treaties require parallel proceedings in every jurisdiction.
Because the line between sovereign and commercial acts is drawn differently in London, New York and Luxembourg.
Because sovereign immunity claims must always be filed in triplicate.
Because bondholders are legally required to sue in their country of citizenship first.
items.e: Textbeleg: „the line between the two continues to be drawn differently in London, New York and Luxembourg, with predictably untidy results for litigants.“

items.q: The bank sought to ____ the embassy's frozen account to satisfy the outstanding judgment.
items.e: „to attach an account“ ist die feste vollstreckungsrechtliche Kollokation; „seize/confiscate“ passen eher zu physischen Gütern im Strafrecht.

items.q: The court granted an order of ____ against the debtor's foreign-held assets.
items.e: „order of attachment“ ist der zivilprozessuale Fachterminus für die Sicherung von Vermögenswerten.

items.q: The bondholders sought to ____ the judgment against assets located in three separate jurisdictions.
items.e: „to enforce a judgment“ ist die Standardkollokation; „execute“ passt eher zu „a sentence“ oder „a warrant“.

items.q: The state's ____ on its sovereign bonds triggered a wave of litigation in three financial centres.
items.e: „default on a bond“ ist die feste finanzrechtliche Kollokation für Zahlungsausfall.

items.q: Foreign ____ filed suit in New York after the government missed its coupon payment.
items.e: „creditors“ = Gläubiger, die eine Forderung geltend machen; „debtors“ wäre der Schuldnerstaat selbst.

items.q: The government argued that issuing the bonds was an act of ____ authority, not a commercial transaction.
items.e: „sovereign authority“ steht im Gegensatz zu „commercial transaction“ — die zentrale Unterscheidung der restriktiven Immunitätsdoktrin.

items.q: The claimant's lawyers argued the transaction was purely ____ in nature and therefore not shielded by immunity.
items.e: „commercial in nature“ ist die feste Fügung, die den Ausnahmetatbestand von der Immunität auslöst.

items.q: Central-bank reserves held abroad typically enjoy a separate layer of ____ from execution.
items.e: „protection from execution“ ist die feste vollstreckungsrechtliche Formel im Text.

items.q: The state formally ____ its immunity from suit when it agreed to New York law arbitration.
items.e: „to waive immunity“ ist die feste rechtliche Kollokation; die übrigen Verben sind zwar sinnverwandt, aber nicht die stehende Fügung im Kontext von Immunitätsverzicht.

items.q: The bank's counsel argued that the ____ did not extend automatically from immunity from suit to immunity from execution.
items.e: „waiver“ ist das feste Substantiv zu „waive“; die übrigen Optionen passen semantisch nicht zum rechtlichen Verzicht auf Immunität.

items.q: The tribunal was asked to rule on the state's plea of ____ immunity from prosecution before the civil courts.
items.e: „absolute immunity“ ist die ältere, umfassendere Doktrin, gegen die sich die restriktive Lehre im Text abgrenzt.

items.q: Courts have moved away from the doctrine under which no suit against a foreign state was ever ____ .
items.e: Nach „was ever“ folgt das Partizip Perfekt als Teil des Passivs: „was ever permitted“.

items.q: The plaintiff obtained a favourable ____ but struggled for years to collect on it.
items.e: „to obtain a judgment“ und „to collect on a judgment“ sind die festen zivilprozessualen Fügungen; „verdict“ betrifft Jury-Entscheidungen im Strafrecht.

items.q: The government's assets abroad proved almost entirely ____ , frustrating the bondholders' judgment.
items.e: „unattachable“ ist das im Text zentrale Fachadjektiv zu „attach“ — nichts konnte gepfändet werden.

items.q: The dispute centred on whether the bond transaction fell within the commercial ____ to immunity.
items.e: „the commercial exception (to immunity)“ ist der stehende Fachbegriff für die Ausnahme bei kommerziellen Geschäften.

items.q: The court held that issuing debt under New York law amounted to a valid waiver of immunity ____ that transaction.
items.e: Feste Rektion: „a waiver for/covering a transaction“ — hier verlangt der Kontext „for“, nicht „of“.

items.q: The defaulting state's legal ____ deepened as more bondholders filed parallel suits abroad.
items.e: „legal exposure“ ist die gebräuchliche Fachkollokation für das Risiko, verklagt zu werden; „liability“ bezeichnet eher die konkrete Haftung selbst.

items.q: The claimants sought to ____ a portion of the state's commercial revenue held in a New York account.
items.e: „to garnish“ = Forderungen gegenüber Dritten pfänden; die einschlägige Vollstreckungstechnik gegenüber Bankguthaben.

items.q: The central bank entered a formal ____ of sovereign immunity to resist the freezing order.
items.e: „to enter a plea of immunity“ ist die feste prozessuale Fügung; „plight“ ist ein Homophon-nahes Substantiv ohne juristische Bedeutung hier.

items.q: Restrictive immunity applies a ____ test to distinguish sovereign from commercial conduct.
items.e: „functional test“ ist der Fachbegriff für die Prüfung der Art der Handlung statt ihres Zwecks.

items.q: The bondholders' claim was ultimately ____ by a New York court applying commercial-activity principles.
items.e: „to uphold a claim“ = einer Klage stattgeben; die übrigen Formen sind keine gebräuchlichen juristischen Verben.

items.q: The bank argued that central-bank ____ , unlike ordinary commercial deposits, could never be attached.
items.e: „central-bank reserves“ ist die im Text zentrale Fachkollokation für die besonders geschützten Vermögenswerte.

items.q: The tribunal found that the transaction, though initiated by the ministry, was ____ commercial.
items.e: „substantively commercial“ = der Sache nach kommerziell; Adverb zur Modifikation des Adjektivs „commercial“.

items.q: The court's ____ jurisdiction over the dispute rested on the commercial-activity exception.
items.e: „subject-matter jurisdiction“ = sachliche Zuständigkeit, hier begründet über die kommerzielle Ausnahme.

items.q: Every ____ before the New York court had raised broadly the same commercial-activity argument.
items.e: „litigant“ = Verfahrenspartei; „litigator“ bezeichnet den Prozessanwalt, nicht die Partei selbst.

items.q: The only ____ still open to the bondholders was to pursue assets in a third jurisdiction.
items.e: „legal remedy“ ist die feste Kollokation für ein Rechtsmittel; „resource“ ist ein False-Friend-Distraktor zum deutschen „Ressource“.

items.q: The court insisted that the state ____ full documentation of the transaction.
items.e: Mandativer Subjunktiv nach „insist that“ — Grundform ohne -s.

items.q: It is imperative that the ruling ____ published before the appeal deadline.
items.e: Mandativer Subjunktiv nach „it is imperative that“ — bloße Grundform „be“.

items.q: Had the bank filed the claim a year earlier, the assets ____ still frozen at trial.
items.e: Typ-3-Konditionalsatz: irreale Vergangenheitsbedingung, Folge ebenfalls in der Vergangenheit.

items.q: If the waiver ____ signed before the default, the creditors could have attached the reserves immediately.
items.e: Typ-3-Konditional: „had been signed“ als irreale Vorzeitigkeit; die Folge „could have attached“ bestätigt den Bezug zur Vergangenheit.

items.q: ____ the tribunal to rule against the state, enforcement would still prove elusive.
items.e: „Were … to rule“ = hypothetische, konditionale Inversion mit „to“-Infinitiv.

items.q: ____ the reserves ever leave the central bank's custody, the creditors' claim would collapse.
items.e: „Should“ + Infinitiv ohne „to“ leitet einen hypothetischen Bedingungssatz mit geringerer Wahrscheinlichkeit ein.

items.q: Little ____ that the waiver would later be contested on execution grounds.
items.e: Negative Inversion nach vorangestelltem „Little“: Hilfsverb vor Subjekt.

items.q: Under no circumstances ____ the reserves be treated as ordinary commercial funds.
items.e: Negative Inversion nach vorangestelltem „Under no circumstances“: Hilfsverb vor Subjekt.

items.q: He told the court that the ministry ____ never authorised the transaction in question.
items.e: Past Perfect nach Backshift in der indirekten Rede (Vorzeitigkeit zum Berichtszeitpunkt).

items.q: The bank stated that the funds ____ be released the following month, not that month.
items.e: Backshift von „will“ zu „would“ in der indirekten Rede; „the following month“ statt „next month“ (Deixisverschiebung).

items.q: The registry ____ have misfiled the waiver; it simply cannot be located.
items.e: „must have“ = logische Gewissheit im Rückblick.

items.q: The bondholders ____ have known that central-bank reserves enjoy separate protection; their filings ignore the distinction entirely.
items.e: „can't have known“ = logische Unmöglichkeit im Rückblick, gestützt durch den nachfolgenden Beleg.

items.q: ____ frustrated the claimants most was the unattachability of the reserves.
items.e: Pseudo-Cleft-Satz: „What … was …“.

items.q: It was the commercial character of the bond, not its sovereign purpose, ____ ultimately settled the case.
items.e: Es-Spaltsatz („It was … that …“) zur Hervorhebung.

items.q: The longer the litigation dragged on, ____ the bondholders' prospects of recovery appeared.
items.e: Korrelative Struktur „the … the …“; der zweite bestimmte Artikel ist obligatorisch.

items.q: The more assets a claimant identifies abroad, ____ the chance of eventual recovery.
items.e: Korrelative Struktur „the … the …“ mit Komparativ im zweiten Satzglied.

items.q: No sooner had the judgment been entered ____ the bondholders moved to attach the account.
items.e: Feste Korrelation „no sooner … than“; „then“ ist Adverb, kein Konnektor.

items.q: Hardly had the reserves been identified ____ the central bank asserted its immunity.
items.e: Feste Korrelation „hardly … when“; nach vorangestelltem „Hardly“ steht die Inversion, danach „when“.

items.q: The bank is said ____ the funds weeks before the freezing order was granted.
items.e: Berichtspassiv mit Vorzeitigkeit: „is said to have moved“.

items.q: The ministry is widely believed ____ the waiver without realising its scope.
items.e: Berichtspassiv „is believed to have signed“ drückt Vorzeitigkeit zum jetzigen Glauben aus.

items.q: ____ under New York law, the bond lost its shield of sovereign immunity for that transaction.
items.e: Passivisches Partizip: die Anleihe wurde begeben, sie begab nicht selbst.

items.q: ____ the restrictive doctrine, several states still resist any narrowing of their immunity.
items.e: „notwithstanding“ + Nominalphrase (ohne „of“); „despite of“ ist falsch, „although“ verlangt einen Nebensatz.

items.q: She read the ruling and ____ immediately.
items.e: Pronominales Objekt „it“ ist nach transitivem „appeal“ (AE-Gebrauch) unmittelbar erforderlich; die Partikelstellung „appealed against it“ ist hier nicht die gesuchte einfache Form.

items.q: The clerk read the filing and ____ before the hearing began.
items.e: Pronominales Objekt „it“ ist nach transitivem „log“ obligatorisch.

items.q: A number of claimants ____ still awaiting a ruling on admissibility.
items.e: „a number of“ + Plural — im Gegensatz zu „the number of“ + Singular.

items.q: The court has yet to rule ____ the immunity of the central bank's reserves.
items.e: Feste Rektion: „rule on“ = entscheiden über; „rule over“ = herrschen über.

items.q: What is the author's principal claim in this passage?
o: ISDS has remained an uncontroversial, technical mechanism throughout its history.
A once-uncontroversial mechanism has become deeply contentious, and reform is now under active multilateral negotiation.
Reform of ISDS was completed decades ago and no longer generates debate.
Host states have universally abandoned investment treaties altogether.
items.e: Kernthese: „It has instead become one of the more contentious features of the treaty system... reform... is now the subject of active multilateral negotiation.“
items.passage:
For thirty years, investor-state dispute settlement was the quiet plumbing of the international economic order: a mechanism, embedded in thousands of treaties, allowing a foreign investor to sue a host government directly before an arbitral tribunal rather than trust to that government's own courts. It was meant to reassure capital that political risk would not go uncompensated. It has instead become one of the more contentious features of the treaty system it was designed to underpin, and reform, once a marginal concern of academic conferences, is now the subject of active multilateral negotiation.

The complaints are by now familiar, if not always fair. Arbitrators, critics note, are drawn from a small pool of practitioners who alternate between sitting as adjudicators and appearing as counsel, an arrangement that would raise eyebrows in any domestic judiciary but has long been tolerated in a system built by and for specialists. Awards have occasionally reached sums that dwarf the annual health budgets of the states ordered to pay them, and the mere threat of a claim, defenders of reform argue, has chilled legitimate regulatory measures on public health and the environment — a phenomenon dubbed regulatory chill, whose scale remains disputed but whose existence few now deny outright.

Two reform paths have gained real traction. One, favoured chiefly in Brussels, would replace ad hoc tribunals with a standing investment court staffed by tenured judges, answerable to an appellate body rather than to the parties who selected them. The other, preferred in Washington and several capitals wary of ceding sovereignty to a permanent bench, would leave the arbitral model largely intact while tightening the substantive standards investors may invoke and narrowing the discretion tribunals enjoy in awarding damages. Neither camp has persuaded the other, and a growing number of states have simply opted out of the system altogether, terminating older treaties rather than waiting for a reform that may never arrive. The result is not consensus but fragmentation — a patchwork in which some investors retain robust protection and others, increasingly, none at all.
items.src: Übungstext im Stil von Foreign Affairs / The Economist (nicht offiziell)

items.q: According to the passage, what does the traditional ISDS mechanism allow a foreign investor to do?
o: Sue the host government directly before an arbitral tribunal rather than trust to that government's own courts.
Appeal exclusively to the United Nations Security Council.
Request compensation only through diplomatic protection by its home state.
Bring criminal charges against host-state officials.
items.e: Textbeleg: „a mechanism... allowing a foreign investor to sue a host government directly before an arbitral tribunal rather than trust to that government's own courts.“

items.q: Why, according to critics, is the pool of ISDS arbitrators problematic?
o: Because arbitrators are never legally trained.
Because arbitrators alternate between sitting as adjudicators and appearing as counsel, an arrangement unusual in domestic judiciaries.
Because arbitrators are appointed exclusively by host states.
Because arbitrators are barred from ever hearing more than one case.
items.e: Textbeleg: „Arbitrators... are drawn from a small pool of practitioners who alternate between sitting as adjudicators and appearing as counsel.“

items.q: What does 'regulatory chill' refer to in the passage?
o: A literal drop in temperature affecting regulatory agencies.
The tendency of the mere threat of an investor claim to discourage legitimate public-health and environmental measures.
A formal moratorium on new investment treaties.
The freezing of an investor's assets pending arbitration.
items.e: Textbeleg: „the mere threat of a claim... has chilled legitimate regulatory measures on public health and the environment — a phenomenon dubbed regulatory chill.“

items.q: What can be inferred about the two reform paths described in the final paragraph?
o: They are identical proposals differing only in name.
They reflect a genuine disagreement over how much sovereignty states should cede to a permanent adjudicative body.
Both have already been unanimously adopted by all treaty parties.
Neither path has attracted support from any government.
items.e: Der Gegensatz „a standing investment court... versus... wary of ceding sovereignty to a permanent bench“ zeigt eine echte Uneinigkeit über den Grad der Souveränitätsabgabe.

items.q: In the phrase 'the quiet plumbing of the international economic order', 'plumbing' is used to suggest that ISDS was originally seen as …
o: a visible and celebrated centrepiece of diplomacy.
an unglamorous but functionally essential background mechanism.
a source of constant public controversy from its inception.
items.e: Metaphorisch: „plumbing“ bezeichnet unauffällige, aber notwendige Infrastruktur — passend zu „quiet“.

items.q: The author's tone in presenting the two reform camps is best described as …
o: strongly partisan in favour of the standing-court model.
dismissive of both proposals as unworkable.
balanced, presenting each camp's position without declaring a winner.
openly mocking of Brussels and Washington alike.
items.e: Beide Reformwege werden sachlich nebeneinandergestellt („Neither camp has persuaded the other“) — ausgewogener, nicht wertender Ton.

items.q: How does the final paragraph relate to the rest of the passage?
o: To announce that a single reform model has been universally adopted.
To show that the absence of agreement between reform camps has produced fragmentation rather than consensus.
To argue that ISDS should be abolished immediately.
To describe the founding of the mechanism in the 1960s.
items.e: Schlussfolgerung: „The result is not consensus but fragmentation — a patchwork...“ — Konsequenz der Uneinigkeit zwischen den Reformlagern.

items.q: The investor initiated ____ proceedings against the host state before a three-member tribunal.
items.e: „arbitral proceedings“ ist die feste Fachkollokation; „arbitrary“ ist ein Homophon-naher False-Friend-Distraktor (willkürlich).

items.q: The tribunal issued an ____ ordering the state to pay several hundred million dollars in compensation.
items.e: „arbitral award“ = Schiedsspruch; „reward“ ist ein False-Friend-Distraktor (Belohnung).

items.q: The dispute was referred to an ad hoc ____ convened under the relevant treaty's arbitration rules.
items.e: „tribunal“ ist der feste Terminus für das mit Investor-Staat-Streitigkeiten befasste Schiedsgericht.

items.q: Brussels favours replacing ad hoc panels with a standing court answerable to an ____ body.
items.e: „appellate body“ = Berufungsinstanz; feste institutionelle Bezeichnung.

items.q: Washington remains wary of ceding ____ to a permanent bench of tenured judges.
items.e: „ceding sovereignty“ ist die im Text zentrale Fügung für den Verzicht auf staatliche Entscheidungshoheit.

items.q: Critics argue the mere threat of a claim has produced a regulatory ____ , discouraging legitimate public-health measures.
items.e: „regulatory chill“ ist der stehende Fachausdruck; die übrigen Optionen sind semantisch verwandt, aber nicht die feste Kollokation.

items.q: The ____ argued that the state's new tobacco-packaging law amounted to indirect expropriation.
items.e: „the investor“ = die klagende Partei im ISDS-Verfahren; die übrigen Formen sind grammatisch unpassend als Subjekt.

items.q: The ____ state maintained that the measure fell squarely within its regulatory prerogative.
items.e: „host state“ = der beklagte Staat, auf dessen Territorium investiert wurde; feste ISDS-Terminologie.

items.q: A growing number of states have terminated the underlying ____ rather than wait for reform.
items.e: „terminate a treaty“ ist die feste völkerrechtliche Kollokation; „treatise“ ist ein Homophon-naher False Friend (wissenschaftliche Abhandlung).

items.q: Several governments have chosen to ____ older treaties rather than await a reform that may never arrive.
items.e: „to terminate a treaty“ = einen Vertrag beenden; „determine“ und „exterminate“ sind Homophon-nahe False-Friend-Distraktoren.

items.q: Awards have occasionally reached ____ that dwarf the annual health budgets of the paying states.
items.e: „sums“ ist die im Text verwendete, idiomatische Kollokation für Geldbeträge in diesem Kontext; die übrigen Optionen sind untypisch für Schadenssummen.

items.q: Arbitrators alternate between sitting as adjudicators and appearing as ____ for one of the parties.
items.e: „counsel“ ist im internationalen Schiedsverfahren der übliche, nationsübergreifende Terminus für den Parteivertreter.

items.q: A standing court would be staffed by tenured judges rather than by party-appointed ____ .
items.e: „adjudicators“ = Entscheidungsträger; die übrigen Formen existieren so nicht im gebräuchlichen Englisch.

items.q: The reform proposal would narrow the ____ tribunals currently enjoy when awarding damages.
items.e: „narrow the discretion“ ist die im Text verwendete Kollokation für eingeschränkten Ermessensspielraum.

items.q: Washington prefers tightening the ____ standards investors may invoke rather than replacing the arbitral model.
items.e: „substantive standards“ = materiell-rechtliche Maßstäbe, im Gegensatz zu verfahrensrechtlichen Fragen.

items.q: The result of the stalled negotiations has been not consensus but ____ across the treaty system.
items.e: „fragmentation“ ist der im Schlussabsatz verwendete Fachbegriff für die uneinheitliche Rechtslage.

items.q: What has emerged is a ____ in which some investors retain robust protection and others none at all.
items.e: „a patchwork of protection“ ist die im Text verwendete Metapher für uneinheitlichen Schutz.

items.q: Several states have simply ____ of the system altogether rather than negotiate reform.
items.e: „to opt out of a system“ ist die feste phrasal-verb-Kollokation für den Austritt.

items.q: The reform debate, once confined to academic conferences, has now gained real ____ in multilateral talks.
items.e: „gain traction“ = an Zugkraft/Zustimmung gewinnen; die übrigen Wörter sind lediglich lautlich ähnlich.

items.q: The proposed court would be staffed by ____ judges rather than by arbitrators selected case by case.
items.e: „tenured judges“ = fest angestellte, auf Dauer berufene Richter; die übrigen Wörter sind lautlich verwandte Distraktoren ohne diese Bedeutung.

items.q: Under the proposed model, judges would be ____ to a permanent appellate body rather than to the parties who selected them.
items.e: „answerable to“ = rechenschaftspflichtig gegenüber; feste adjektivische Fügung.

items.q: Some awards have grown large enough to ____ the annual health budgets of the states ordered to pay them.
items.e: „to dwarf something“ = etwas weit übertreffen an Größe; feste Kollokation im Text.

items.q: The dual role of arbitrators as both judges and advocates has raised ____ among observers of domestic judiciaries.
items.e: „to raise eyebrows“ = Verwunderung/Kritik hervorrufen; feste idiomatische Wendung.

items.q: Arbitrators are drawn from a small ____ of practitioners who know one another well.
items.e: „a small pool of practitioners“ ist die feste Kollokation für einen begrenzten Kreis von Fachleuten.

items.q: Defenders of reform argue that the mere ____ of a claim can chill legitimate regulation before any tribunal even convenes.
items.e: „the mere threat of a claim“ ist die im Text zentrale Nominalphrase.

items.q: A losing party may petition a domestic court to ____ the award on narrow procedural grounds.
items.e: „to vacate an award“ = einen Schiedsspruch gerichtlich aufheben; nicht zu verwechseln mit „evacuate“ (evakuieren).

items.q: The treaty requires that the tribunal ____ its award within a fixed period.
items.e: Mandativer Subjunktiv nach „require that“ — Grundform ohne -s.

items.q: It is essential that the arbitrator ____ free of any conflicting appointment.
items.e: Mandativer Subjunktiv nach „it is essential that“ — bloße Grundform „be“.

items.q: Had the state ratified the reform protocol earlier, the tribunal ____ under the new rules.
items.e: Typ-3-Konditionalsatz: irreale Vergangenheitsbedingung, Folge ebenfalls in der Vergangenheit.

items.q: If the claim ____ filed a year earlier, the award would already be final today.
items.e: Gemischter Konditionalsatz: Bedingung in der Vergangenheit, Folge in der Gegenwart („today“).

items.q: ____ the appellate body to overturn the award, the entire reform would lose credibility.
items.e: „Were … to overturn“ = hypothetische, konditionale Inversion mit „to“-Infinitiv.

items.q: ____ the negotiations collapse, several states would likely withdraw from the treaty altogether.

items.q: What is the author's principal claim about universal jurisdiction?
o: Universal jurisdiction is a simple doctrine that has always been applied consistently everywhere.
Universal jurisdiction sounds simple in principle but has proved difficult to apply, and its scope has been narrowed by several states in practice.
No state has ever attempted to prosecute a foreign national under universal jurisdiction.
Piracy prosecutions ended the practical use of universal jurisdiction entirely.
items.e: Kernthese: „rests on a proposition that sounds simple until one tries to apply it“; im dritten Absatz wird die praktische Einschränkung beschrieben.
items.passage:
Universal jurisdiction rests on a proposition that sounds simple until one tries to apply it: certain crimes are so grave that any state, regardless of where the offence occurred or the nationality of victim or perpetrator, may prosecute the offender if he is ever found within its territory. The doctrine has an old pedigree — piracy on the high seas has been triable everywhere for centuries — but its extension to torture, war crimes and crimes against humanity is a comparatively recent, and still contested, development.

National courts that have taken the doctrine seriously have found themselves navigating a thicket of practical and diplomatic obstacles largely absent from ordinary criminal trials. Evidence must typically be gathered on foreign soil, often years after the events in question and frequently in states unwilling to cooperate with an investigation implicating their own former or serving officials. Witnesses must be persuaded to travel, or their testimony taken by video link under procedures that defence counsel routinely challenge. And prosecutors must reckon with the diplomatic fallout of indicting a foreign national, a step that has more than once provoked the recall of ambassadors and the freezing of bilateral cooperation on unrelated matters.

Several states that once embraced an expansive version of the doctrine have since narrowed it considerably, typically by requiring some jurisdictional link — residence, presence, or a victim of the forum state's own nationality — rather than allowing prosecutions to proceed in absentia against defendants who have never set foot in the country. Advocates regard the retreat as a capitulation to political pressure from states eager to shield their own nationals; sceptics regard it as a necessary correction, restoring a measure of realism to a doctrine whose earlier, more ambitious form risked turning national courts into forums for prosecutions they lacked the practical means to conduct fairly. What both camps concede is that the handful of convictions secured to date, however hard-won, have done more to vindicate the principle than any number of unexecuted arrest warrants ever could.
items.src: Übungstext im Stil von Foreign Affairs / The Economist (nicht offiziell)

items.q: According to the passage, which offence has long been triable everywhere under the doctrine's oldest form?
items.e: Textbeleg: „piracy on the high seas has been triable everywhere for centuries.“

items.q: What practical obstacle do national courts face when gathering evidence under universal jurisdiction?
o: Evidence is always readily available within the prosecuting state's own borders.
Evidence must typically be gathered on foreign soil, often in states unwilling to cooperate.
Courts are legally forbidden from ever collecting evidence abroad.
Only written evidence, never witness testimony, is admissible.

items.q: What can be inferred about states that once embraced an expansive version of the doctrine?
o: They have since narrowed it, typically by requiring a jurisdictional link such as residence or presence.
They have abolished all forms of criminal jurisdiction over foreign nationals.
They have extended the doctrine to cover ordinary civil disputes.
They now require unanimous UN Security Council approval before any prosecution.
items.e: Textbeleg: „Several states that once embraced an expansive version of the doctrine have since narrowed it considerably, typically by requiring some jurisdictional link.“

items.q: In the phrase 'a thicket of practical and diplomatic obstacles', 'thicket' is used to mean …
o: a dense, tangled mass of literal vegetation surrounding courtrooms.
a complicated, difficult-to-navigate set of obstacles.
a formal legal document listing procedural rules.
a small committee established to review evidence.
items.e: Metaphorisch: „a thicket of obstacles“ = ein verworrenes, schwer zu durchdringendes Geflecht von Hindernissen.

items.q: The author's tone toward the debate between advocates and sceptics of the doctrine's retreat is best described as …

dismissive of both positions as naïve.
even-handed, presenting both the advocates' and the sceptics' arguments.
triumphant that the doctrine has been fully vindicated.
items.e: Beide Positionen werden nebeneinandergestellt („Advocates regard the retreat as... sceptics regard it as...“) ohne eindeutige Parteinahme.

items.q: What is the primary function of the final sentence of the passage?

To suggest that both advocates and sceptics agree the handful of convictions secured has done more to vindicate the principle than unexecuted warrants.
To announce the doctrine's complete abandonment.
To describe a newly signed international convention on piracy.
items.e: Textbeleg: „What both camps concede is that the handful of convictions secured to date... have done more to vindicate the principle than any number of unexecuted arrest warrants.“

items.q: What is the central argument advanced by the author?
o: Restitution claims have moved from the margins of museum policy to its centre within roughly a decade.
Museums have never faced any restitution claims for colonial-era acquisitions.
Restitution claims are always backed by decades of archival research.
Courts across all jurisdictions apply an identical limitation-period rule to restitution claims.
items.e: Kernthese im ersten Satz: „has moved, within little more than a decade, from the margins of museum policy to the centre of it.“
items.passage:
The return of cultural objects removed from their countries of origin under conditions ranging from outright plunder to legally ambiguous colonial-era acquisition has moved, within little more than a decade, from the margins of museum policy to the centre of it. Institutions that once treated their collections as permanent and largely unquestionable now face a steady stream of restitution claims, some backed by decades of painstaking archival research, others resting on little more than the presumption that objects taken during a period of conquest were unlikely to have changed hands willingly.

The legal terrain claimants must cross is notoriously uneven. Limitation periods, designed for ordinary property disputes, sit awkwardly with claims arising from events a century or more in the past, and courts in different jurisdictions have reached sharply divergent conclusions about when the clock on such a claim should be deemed to start running. Some have held that it begins only once the current possessor's identity and location become known to the claimant; others have applied the ordinary rule strictly, effectively barring claims however compelling the underlying evidence of wrongful taking. Good-faith purchase doctrines complicate matters further still, since several legal systems protect a buyer who acquired an object without knowledge of its tainted provenance, regardless of how clearly that provenance can now be established.

Faced with this thicket, many institutions have chosen to bypass litigation altogether, negotiating voluntary returns or long-term loan arrangements that allow an object to travel back to its claimed community of origin without a court ever pronouncing on legal title. Critics regard such settlements as an admission dressed up as generosity; defenders counter that they achieve in months what contested litigation might not resolve in a decade, and that the objects themselves are better served by return than by a legal victory that leaves them permanently in dispute. Whichever view one takes, the direction of travel is unmistakable: claims once dismissed out of hand are now, at the very least, taken seriously enough to negotiate over.
items.src: Übungstext im Stil von Foreign Affairs / The Economist (nicht offiziell)

items.q: According to the passage, what complicates the application of ordinary limitation periods to restitution claims?
o: Limitation periods were specifically designed for restitution claims and fit them perfectly.
Limitation periods, designed for ordinary property disputes, sit awkwardly with claims arising from events a century or more in the past.
Restitution claims are exempt from all limitation periods everywhere.
Museums are legally required to waive limitation defences automatically.
items.e: Textbeleg: „Limitation periods, designed for ordinary property disputes, sit awkwardly with claims arising from events a century or more in the past.“

items.q: How do courts differ regarding when the limitation clock begins to run on a restitution claim?
o: All courts agree it begins the moment the object was originally taken.
Some hold it begins only once the possessor's identity becomes known to the claimant; others apply the ordinary rule strictly, barring claims regardless of evidence.
No court has ever ruled on when a restitution claim's limitation period begins.
Courts uniformly refuse to apply any limitation period to restitution claims.
items.e: Textbeleg: „Some have held that it begins only once the current possessor's identity and location become known...; others have applied the ordinary rule strictly, effectively barring claims.“

items.q: What can be inferred about many institutions' recent approach to restitution disputes?
o: They have chosen to bypass litigation altogether, negotiating voluntary returns or loan arrangements instead.
They have refused to engage with any claimant under any circumstances.
They have unanimously agreed to return every contested object immediately.
They have insisted that only courts, never negotiation, can resolve such disputes.
items.e: Textbeleg: „many institutions have chosen to bypass litigation altogether, negotiating voluntary returns or long-term loan arrangements.“

items.q: In the phrase 'an admission dressed up as generosity', 'dressed up as' is used to mean …
o: presented misleadingly in the guise of.
items.e: „dressed up as“ = fälschlich/beschönigend dargestellt als; Kritikerperspektive, die die Rückgabe als verkapptes Schuldeingeständnis deutet.

items.q: The author's tone toward the dispute between critics and defenders of voluntary settlements is best described as …
o: strongly partisan in favour of the critics.
dismissive of both positions as unserious.
balanced, presenting both critics' and defenders' arguments without declaring a winner.
openly hostile toward museums as an institution.
items.e: Beide Sichtweisen werden nebeneinandergestellt („Critics regard... defenders counter...“) ohne klare Parteinahme.

items.q: What purpose does the passage's closing sentence serve?
o: To argue that all restitution claims will soon be rejected by every court.
To conclude that claims once dismissed out of hand are now taken seriously enough to negotiate over.
To summarise the legal history of limitation periods in property law.
To announce a binding international treaty on cultural restitution.
items.e: Textbeleg: „the direction of travel is unmistakable: claims once dismissed out of hand are now, at the very least, taken seriously enough to negotiate over.“

items.q: Why do good-faith purchase doctrines complicate restitution claims, according to the passage?
o: Because they protect a buyer who acquired an object without knowledge of its tainted provenance, regardless of how clearly that provenance can now be established.
Because they automatically transfer legal title back to the original claimant.
Because they apply only to objects acquired within the last five years.
Because they have been abolished in every major legal system.
items.e: Textbeleg: „several legal systems protect a buyer who acquired an object without knowledge of its tainted provenance, regardless of how clearly that provenance can now be established.“

items.q: Many objects now claimed were removed under conditions amounting to outright ____ during periods of conquest.
items.e: „outright plunder“ ist die im Text verwendete Kollokation; die übrigen Optionen sind grammatisch unpassend oder untypisch.

items.q: Establishing an object's ____ has become central to any restitution claim.

items.q: The ____ argued that decades of archival research supported the claim's underlying facts.

items.q: Ordinary ____ periods were never designed with century-old claims of this kind in mind.

items.q: The claimant alleged ____ taking during a period when the territory was under foreign occupation.
items.e: „wrongful taking“ ist die feste Fachkollokation für widerrechtliche Wegnahme.

items.q: Several legal systems apply a ____ purchase doctrine that protects an unwitting buyer.
items.e: „good-faith purchase“ ist der stehende Fachbegriff für den gutgläubigen Erwerb.

items.q: A court must ultimately decide who holds legal ____ to the disputed object.
items.e: „legal title“ ist die im Text verwendete Fachkollokation für das Eigentumsrecht.

items.q: Some institutions have opted for ____ returns rather than face protracted litigation.
items.e: „voluntary returns“ ist die im Text verwendete adjektivische Kollokation.

items.q: A long-term ____ arrangement can allow an object to travel home without a formal transfer of title.
items.e: „a loan arrangement“ ist die im Text zentrale Kollokation für die zeitweise Rückgabe ohne Titelübertragung.

items.q: The museum reached a negotiated ____ that avoided a formal ruling on legal title.
items.e: „a negotiated settlement“ ist die im Text zentrale Kollokation.

items.q: Critics regard such returns as an admission ____ as generosity.
items.e: „dressed up as“ ist die im Text verwendete idiomatische Wendung für eine beschönigende Darstellung.

items.q: Some claims rest on decades of ____ research into shipping records and auction catalogues.
items.e: „archival research“ ist die im Text verwendete adjektivische Kollokation.

items.q: Establishing provenance across a century often requires ____ , painstaking work by specialist researchers.
items.e: „painstaking work“ = mühsame, akribische Arbeit; die übrigen Formen sind keine gebräuchlichen englischen Wörter.

items.q: Some claims rest on little more than the ____ that objects taken during conquest changed hands unwillingly.

items.q: Which of the following best summarises the author's main point?
o: Diplomatic immunity has never generated any public controversy.
The remedies the Vienna Convention provides are adequate on paper but exercised far less often than credible allegations would suggest.
Every diplomat accused of a crime is automatically prosecuted upon returning home.
Receiving states have lost the legal power to expel diplomatic staff.
items.e: Kernthese im zweiten Absatz: „the remedies... are, on paper, adequate to the problem... In practice, both remedies are exercised far less often than the frequency of credible allegations would suggest.“
items.passage:
Diplomatic immunity exists, the Vienna Convention makes plain, not to excuse the individual envoy but to protect the function he performs; a diplomat who commits an offence remains formally guilty of it even though the receiving state's courts have no power to try him. That distinction, elegant in a law-school seminar, has proved considerably harder to sustain in public debate whenever a mission employee is credibly accused of a serious crime and promptly departs the country beyond the reach of any local court whatsoever.

The remedies the Convention itself provides are, on paper, adequate to the problem: the receiving state may declare the individual persona non grata, compelling recall, and the sending state remains free — indeed formally encouraged — to waive immunity or to prosecute the individual under its own law once he returns home. In practice, both remedies are exercised far less often than the frequency of credible allegations would suggest. Waiver requires a sending government to concede, in effect, that one of its own officials may have committed a serious crime abroad, a concession most foreign ministries are reluctant to make regardless of the evidence, and prosecution at home depends on a domestic legal system willing to pursue a case whose evidence and witnesses remain, inconveniently, in another country entirely.

Reform proposals have periodically surfaced — automatic waiver clauses for the gravest offences, insurance schemes to compensate victims regardless of whether prosecution ever follows, faster and more transparent expulsion procedures — yet none has attracted the near-universal ratification that would be needed to close the gap uniformly. Receiving states, for their part, have grown more willing to expel diplomatic staff even absent a waiver, accepting the diplomatic cost of a strained bilateral relationship as preferable to the alternative of visible impunity playing out in the domestic press. The underlying tension, between a rule that protects an indispensable function and a public that increasingly experiences it as protecting the individual instead, shows no sign of resolving itself soon.
items.src: Übungstext im Stil von Foreign Affairs / The Economist (nicht offiziell)

items.q: According to the passage, what does the Vienna Convention's distinction actually protect?

The function the diplomat performs, not the individual as such.

Receiving states never request waivers in practice.
items.e: Textbeleg: „Waiver requires a sending government to concede, in effect, that one of its own officials may have committed a serious crime abroad, a concession most foreign ministries are reluctant to make.“

o: They have grown more willing to expel staff even absent a waiver, accepting the diplomatic cost as preferable to visible impunity.

items.q: In the phrase 'elegant in a law-school seminar', the author implies that the function/individual distinction is …

theoretically neat but difficult to sustain once a serious allegation becomes public.
irrelevant to how courts actually rule.
items.e: Textbeleg: „That distinction, elegant in a law-school seminar, has proved considerably harder to sustain in public debate.“
