items.q: What is the author's central argument about defence procurement failures?
o: They are caused solely by incompetent engineers.
They stem predictably from political incentives that reward launching programmes more than completing them well.
They have been entirely solved by fixed-price contracts.
They only occur in countries without domestic arms industries.
items.e: Schlusssatz: „procurement dysfunction is not a technical failure... but the predictable output of political incentives that reward starting programmes considerably more than they reward finishing them well.“
items.passage:
Every major arms programme, it sometimes seems, is destined to arrive late, over budget, and diminished in ambition from whatever was originally promised. The pattern is so familiar that defence ministries have developed an entire vocabulary to soften its recurrence — 'schedule slippage,' 'cost growth,' 'capability trade-offs' — euphemisms that describe, with admirable delicacy, the gap between what was procured and what was paid for. Explaining the pattern is easier than curing it, which may be why so many inquiries reach broadly the same conclusions and so few programmes subsequently improve.

Part of the difficulty is structural. Requirements are drawn up years, sometimes a decade, before a platform enters service, during which the threat environment, available technology and political priorities can all shift beyond recognition. Contractors, aware that the customer has limited alternatives once a programme is under way, have little incentive to resist expanding requirements that pad both timeline and price. Governments, for their part, are reluctant to cancel a programme that has already absorbed years of investment, however unpromising its trajectory — a variant of the sunk-cost fallacy that procurement officials recognise perfectly well and are nonetheless powerless to escape.

Industrial policy complicates matters further. Few governments are willing to buy the objectively best available platform if it means idling a domestic production line and the jobs that depend on it; national champions are protected not because they build the cheapest equipment but because the alternative is politically unpalatable. The resulting fragmentation — a continent fielding a dozen incompatible armoured-vehicle designs where two or three would suffice — imposes a hidden tax on every subsequent joint operation, measured in incompatible spare parts and duplicated training pipelines.

Reformers periodically propose remedies: fixed-price contracts, competitive prototyping, harsher penalties for delay. Each has merit; none has proved sufficient on its own. What the record suggests, more soberingly, is that procurement dysfunction is not a technical failure awaiting a technical fix but the predictable output of political incentives that reward starting programmes considerably more than they reward finishing them well.
items.src: Übungstext im Stil von Foreign Affairs / The Economist (nicht offiziell)

items.q: What does the author say about terms like 'schedule slippage' and 'cost growth'?
o: They are precise legal definitions used in contracts.
They are euphemisms that soften the description of the gap between promise and delivery.
They refer exclusively to naval programmes.
They were invented by journalists, not ministries.
items.e: „euphemisms that describe, with admirable delicacy, the gap between what was procured and what was paid for.“

items.q: According to the passage, why are contractors reluctant to resist expanding requirements?
o: They are legally obliged to expand requirements.
The customer has limited alternatives once a programme is under way, reducing pressure to resist.
Expanding requirements always lowers their profit.
Governments forbid contractors from raising concerns.
items.e: „aware that the customer has limited alternatives once a programme is under way, have little incentive to resist expanding requirements.“

items.q: What can be inferred about governments' reluctance to cancel failing programmes?
o: It reflects a rational recalculation of future costs and benefits.
It resembles a sunk-cost fallacy, continuing investment because of what has already been spent.
It is required by international law.
It only happens with naval programmes.
items.e: „a variant of the sunk-cost fallacy that procurement officials recognise perfectly well and are nonetheless powerless to escape.“

items.q: 'Idling a domestic production line' most nearly means …
o: leaving a factory without work or use.
selling a factory to a foreign buyer.
items.e: „idle“ = stillstehen/brachliegen (eine Fabrik ohne Auftrag).

items.q: The author's tone towards proposed procurement reforms (fixed-price contracts, competitive prototyping) is …
o: fully convinced they will solve the problem.
cautiously sceptical that any single measure suffices.
dismissive, considering all reform proposals worthless.
items.e: „Each has merit; none has proved sufficient on its own.“

items.q: What is the function of the third paragraph (beginning 'Industrial policy complicates matters further')?
o: To argue that industrial policy is entirely unrelated to procurement problems.
To explain how protecting domestic production leads to fragmented, incompatible equipment across a continent.
To list every armoured-vehicle design currently in production.
To praise national champions for their efficiency.
items.e: Erklärt, wie der Schutz nationaler Produktion zu fragmentierter, inkompatibler Ausrüstung führt.

items.q: What hidden cost does the author attribute to equipment fragmentation?
o: Incompatible spare parts and duplicated training pipelines during joint operations.
items.e: „imposes a hidden tax on every subsequent joint operation, measured in incompatible spare parts and duplicated training pipelines.“

items.q: The programme suffered repeated schedule ____ , pushing delivery back by nearly a decade.
items.e: Feste Fügung „schedule slippage“, korrekte Substantivform.

items.q: Cost ____ on the fighter programme has more than doubled the original estimate.
items.e: „a cost overrun“ (Singular) stimmt mit dem Verb „has“ überein; das Plural „overruns“ würde „have“ verlangen — feiner Kongruenzunterschied.

items.q: The ministry opted for a ____ contract to shift financial risk onto the contractor.
items.e: „fixed-price contract“ ist der Standardbegriff im Beschaffungswesen; „flat-rate“ gehört eher ins Konsumenten-/Telekomregister.

items.q: Several bidders were invited to submit competing designs under a ____ prototyping scheme.
items.e: Korrekte Adjektivform vor „prototyping“; die übrigen Optionen sind grammatisch die falsche Wortart in dieser Position.

items.q: The shipyard's order book depends heavily on a single ____ contract from the navy.
items.e: „sole-source contract“ ist der feste Fachbegriff für eine nicht-kompetitive Auftragsvergabe.

items.q: Domestic production lines were kept running to protect jobs, even though the imported alternative was markedly ____ .
items.e: Logischer Kontrast durch „even though“: die einheimische Option ist teurer, die importierte billiger.

items.q: The fragmented market leaves the continent fielding a dozen ____ armoured-vehicle designs.
items.e: „incompatible“ ist der präzise technische Fachbegriff für nicht kompatible Ausrüstung.

items.q: The inquiry attributed the delay to poorly defined ____ drawn up a decade before deployment.
items.e: Feste Kollokation „poorly defined requirements“.

items.q: Analysts describe the sunk-cost ____ as the chief reason failing programmes are rarely cancelled.
items.e: „sunk-cost fallacy“ ist der feststehende ökonomische Fachbegriff.

items.q: The two allied air forces cannot share spare parts because their fleets are simply not ____ .
items.e: „interchangeable parts“ ist die präzise technische Kollokation.

items.q: The contractor was accused of ____ costs by inflating the bill of materials.
items.e: Idiom „to pad costs/expenses“ = Kosten künstlich aufblähen.

items.q: National ____ are protected by governments reluctant to see high-skilled manufacturing jobs disappear.
items.e: „national champions“ ist der feste industriepolitische Fachbegriff.

items.q: The armoured vehicle finally entered ____ after years of delay.
items.e: Feste Kollokation „enter service“.

items.q: Procurement officials have long recognised the problem but remain ____ to escape its underlying incentives.
items.e: Idiomatische Wendung „powerless to escape“.

items.q: The shipbuilder's order book depends on maintaining a steady production ____ rather than a single large batch.
items.e: „production cadence“ ist ein spezifischer moderner Fachbegriff der Rüstungs-/Fertigungsindustrie.

items.q: Governments have grown wary of ____ contractors, given the sector's history of consolidation.
items.e: Korrekte Adjektivform vor „contractors“.

items.q: The tender attracted only a single bid, raising concerns about a lack of ____ in the sector.
items.e: „lack of competition“ bezieht sich auf das Fehlen konkurrierender Anbieter, nicht auf Wettbewerbsfähigkeit als Eigenschaft.

items.q: The armoured-vehicle programme was ultimately ____ after costs tripled the original estimate.
items.e: „scrapped“ ist der Standardbegriff für die Einstellung eines Programms; „scrubbed“ wird eher für den Abbruch eines einzelnen Starts/einer Mission verwendet.

items.q: The audit found that the ministry had failed to ____ the contractor's financial stability before signing.
items.e: „vet“ ist der idiomatische Fachbegriff für die Prüfung der Eignung/Zuverlässigkeit eines Vertragspartners.

items.q: The two ministries agreed to ____ their procurement budgets for the joint fighter programme.
items.e: Idiom „pool resources/budgets“.

items.q: The contractor was blacklisted after evidence of ____ in the bidding process emerged.
items.e: „collusion in bidding“ (Angebotsabsprache) ist der präzise Fachbegriff.

items.q: The new frigate design underwent extensive ____ before entering series production.
items.e: Feststehender Fachbegriff „sea trials“ = Seeerprobung.

items.q: The company's ____ of the missile system fell well short of the specification.
items.e: „performance“ ist der technische Fachbegriff für das Leistungsverhalten gegenüber der Spezifikation.

items.q: The ministry imposed financial ____ for every month the delivery ran late.
items.e: „penalties“ passt am besten ins vertragsrechtliche Beschaffungsregister; „sanctions“ suggeriert eher außenpolitische Maßnahmen.

items.q: Reformers have called for stricter ____ mechanisms to deter chronic delay.
items.e: „enforcement mechanisms“ ist die feste Fachfügung.

items.q: The shipyard's workforce depends on a steady ____ of naval orders to remain viable.
items.e: „order pipeline“ ist der gängige moderne industriepolitische Fachbegriff.

items.q: The auditor recommended that the ministry ____ the contract before further funds were released.
items.e: Mandativer Subjunktiv nach „recommend that“ — Grundform ohne -s.

items.q: Had the ministry cancelled the programme sooner, taxpayers ____ far less today.
items.e: Gemischter Konditional: Bedingung Vergangenheit, Folge Gegenwart.

items.q: ____ costs to double again, parliament would almost certainly demand the programme's cancellation.
items.e: „Were … to“ — invertierte hypothetische Zukunftsform.

items.q: No sooner had the contract been signed ____ the specifications began to change.
items.e: Feste Korrelation „no sooner … than“.

items.q: The delay ____ have been foreseen; the risk register flagged the supplier's history months earlier.
items.e: „should have + Partizip“ = Kritik an einer versäumten, vorhersehbaren Handlung.

items.q: The shipyard ____ its final invoice only last week.
items.e: Abgeschlossener Zeitpunkt („last week“) schließt das Present Perfect aus.

items.q: By the time the frigate is commissioned, the programme ____ for nearly fifteen years.
items.e: Future Perfect nach „by the time“ bei andauernder Handlung.

items.q: A range of suppliers ____ competing for the contract.
items.e: „a range of“ + Plural.

items.q: The longer the tender dragged on, ____ the shortlisted bidders became.
items.e: Korrelative Struktur „the … the …“ verlangt zwei Artikel.

items.q: The committee redacted the cost figures ____ they prejudice the ongoing negotiation.
items.e: „lest“ + Subjunktiv (Grundform).

items.q: ____ frustrated auditors most was not the overrun itself but the ministry's reluctance to explain it.
items.e: Pseudo-Cleft „What … was …“.

items.q: Engineers tested the prototype and ____ before the deadline.
items.e: Pronominales Objekt steht zwingend zwischen Verb und Partikel.

items.q: The contractor is understood ____ the specification without informing the ministry.
items.e: Berichtspassiv mit Vorzeitigkeit: „is understood to have altered“.

items.q: Having secured the initial contract, the firm went on ____ two further follow-on orders.
items.e: „go on to do“ = zu einer neuen Handlung übergehen.

items.q: The minister would rather the announcement ____ until the audit concluded.
items.e: „would rather“ + Simple Past bei Gegenwarts-/Zukunftsbezug.

items.q: The clause ____ the contractor objected has since been rewritten.
items.e: Vorangestellte Präposition verlangt „which“, nie „that“.

items.q: ____ under intense budgetary pressure, the design was stripped of several planned capabilities.
items.e: Passivisches Partizip; die Aktivform würde die Konstruktion zum Handelnden machen.

items.q: The final cost was ____ higher than the figure originally presented to parliament.
items.e: Adverb modifiziert das Adjektiv „higher“.

items.q: The contractor had promised delivery ____ ; the deadline came and went.
items.e: Deixisverschiebung in der Redewiedergabe: „next spring“ → „the following spring“.

items.q: ____ did the programme run late, but it also delivered fewer units than promised.
items.e: „Not only … but also“ verlangt Inversion nach vorangestelltem „Not only“.

items.q: Hardly had the first unit rolled off the line ____ a design flaw was discovered.
items.e: „hardly … when“ (im Unterschied zu „no sooner … than“).

items.q: The spokesperson described the launch as though every milestone ____ already met.
items.e: „as though“ + Past Perfect bei Bezug auf eine vorzeitige, irreale Situation.

items.q: The ministry ____ have rushed the announcement; the contract was not due to be signed for weeks.
items.e: „needn't have + Partizip“ = unnötige, aber tatsächlich ausgeführte Handlung.

items.q: He was appointed ____ chief procurement officer shortly after the scandal broke.
items.e: Nullartikel vor einmaligen Ämtern nach „appoint“.

items.q: The report's criticism bears directly ____ the ministry's oversight failures.
items.e: „bear on“ = betreffen.

items.q: The board insisted that the contractor ____ compensation for every month of delay.
items.e: Mandativer Subjunktiv nach „insist that“.

items.q: What is the central tension the author identifies in state cyber-attack attribution?
o: Attribution is always scientifically certain and therefore uncontroversial.
Governments increasingly attribute attacks publicly even though supporting evidence often cannot be disclosed, raising credibility questions.
No government has ever publicly attributed a cyber-attack.
Attribution disputes are purely a technical, not political, matter.
items.e: „That last point is the crux of the credibility problem. Citizens and allied governments alike are asked to trust an accusation whose supporting evidence remains, by necessity, classified.“
items.passage:
When a hospital's systems freeze, a pipeline's pumps stop, or a ministry's servers begin leaking classified cables, the question that follows within hours is rarely whether an attack occurred but who is responsible for it. The answer, more often than the public appreciates, resists easy proof. Digital evidence can be spoofed, routed through compromised servers in a third country, and dressed in the coding habits of a rival service specifically to mislead investigators — a manoeuvre intelligence agencies call a false flag, borrowed from the naval practice of sailing under another nation's colours to deceive an enemy.

Governments nonetheless attribute attacks with growing confidence, and growing speed. Part of the explanation is technical: forensic firms have built vast libraries of malware samples, infrastructure fingerprints and operational patterns that allow a given intrusion to be matched, with reasonable confidence, to a known group. Part of the explanation is political: an attribution statement is itself a diplomatic instrument, a way of imposing reputational cost on an adversary without firing a shot, and governments have grown more willing to make such statements even where the underlying evidence cannot be published without compromising sources.

That last point is the crux of the credibility problem. Citizens and allied governments alike are asked to trust an accusation whose supporting evidence remains, by necessity, classified. Sceptics note that this arrangement leaves considerable room for politically convenient attribution — accusations timed to coincide with sanctions votes or elections, levelled against adversaries already unpopular for unrelated reasons. Defenders counter that joint statements, co-signed by a widening circle of allied intelligence services, provide at least a rough proxy for rigour that no single government could offer alone.

Neither position fully resolves the dilemma. What has changed, unmistakably, is the willingness of victim states to name names publicly rather than absorb an intrusion in silence, calculating that the reputational cost imposed on an accused aggressor, however imperfectly substantiated, now outweighs the diplomatic awkwardness of making an accusation that cannot be proven beyond doubt.
items.src: Übungstext im Stil von Foreign Affairs / The Economist (nicht offiziell)

items.q: What is a 'false flag' operation, as described in the passage?
o: An attack openly claimed by the attacking state.
An attack disguised to implicate a different actor, borrowing the coding habits of a rival service.
A diplomatic protest lodged after an attack.
A defensive measure used to block intrusions.
items.e: „dressed in the coding habits of a rival service specifically to mislead investigators — a manoeuvre intelligence agencies call a false flag.“

items.q: According to the passage, why have forensic firms grown more confident in attribution?
o: Because all attackers now confess voluntarily.
Because they have built extensive libraries of malware samples and infrastructure patterns for matching intrusions.
Because international law requires public evidence disclosure.
Because attacks have become technically simpler.
items.e: „forensic firms have built vast libraries of malware samples, infrastructure fingerprints and operational patterns that allow a given intrusion to be matched... to a known group.“

items.q: What can be inferred about sceptics' concerns regarding attribution statements?
o: They believe attribution is always fabricated entirely.
They worry that classified evidence allows politically convenient timing of accusations.
They think attribution statements are legally binding.
They believe only military tribunals can attribute attacks.
items.e: „this arrangement leaves considerable room for politically convenient attribution — accusations timed to coincide with sanctions votes or elections.“

items.q: 'A rough proxy for rigour' most nearly means …
o: an exact scientific measurement of certainty.
an imperfect but useful substitute indicator of thoroughness.
a legal requirement under international law.
items.e: „proxy“ hier übertragen: unvollkommener Ersatzindikator, keine exakte Messung.

items.q: The author's tone in presenting both sceptics' and defenders' arguments is best described as …
o: balanced, presenting both positions without fully endorsing either.
openly hostile towards allied intelligence services.
uncritically supportive of every government attribution.
items.e: Beide Positionen (Sceptics/Defenders) werden gleichwertig referiert, ohne dass der Autor eindeutig Partei ergreift.

items.q: What is the function of the final paragraph?
o: To resolve the credibility dilemma definitively in favour of victim states.
To note that neither position fully resolves the dilemma, while explaining why victim states now attribute publicly more often.
To introduce a new historical case study.
To argue that attribution should never be made public.
items.e: „Neither position fully resolves the dilemma. What has changed, unmistakably, is the willingness of victim states to name names publicly.“

items.q: Why, according to the passage, do victim states increasingly 'name names' publicly?
o: Because international courts now require it.
Because they calculate the reputational cost imposed on the accused now outweighs the awkwardness of an unproven accusation.
Because forensic evidence has become impossible to fake.
items.e: „calculating that the reputational cost imposed on an accused aggressor... now outweighs the diplomatic awkwardness of making an accusation that cannot be proven beyond doubt.“

items.q: Investigators struggled to ____ the attack to a specific state actor without compromising their sources.
items.e: Feste Kollokation „attribute X to Y“ ist der Standardbegriff in Cyber-/Geheimdienstberichten.

items.q: The malware's code bore telltale ____ linking it to a known hacking group.
items.e: „malware signature“ = digitales Erkennungsmuster, feststehender IT-Sicherheits-Fachbegriff.

items.q: The operation was designed as a ____ , disguised to implicate a rival intelligence service.
items.e: Feststehender Fachbegriff „false flag operation“.

items.q: Servers in a third country were used to ____ the true origin of the intrusion.
items.e: „obfuscate“ ist der spezifische IT-Sicherheits-Fachbegriff für die gezielte Verschleierung von Code/Herkunft; die anderen sind allgemeinsprachliche Synonyme.

items.q: The ministry's servers were found to be ____ , allowing the intruders unrestricted lateral movement.
items.e: „compromised“ ist der Standardbegriff der IT-Sicherheit für ein kompromittiertes System.

items.q: The joint statement was ____ by a dozen allied intelligence services.
items.e: „co-signed“ ist die feste Kollokation für gemeinsam unterzeichnete Erklärungen.

items.q: The attack exploited a previously unknown ____ in the software.
items.e: „vulnerability“ ist der präzise Fachbegriff der IT-Sicherheit.

items.q: The intrusion remained undetected for months, a so-called ____ threat embedded deep within the network.
items.e: „advanced persistent threat (APT)“ ist der feste Fachbegriff.

items.q: Analysts traced the command-and-control ____ back to a server farm in a third country.
items.e: „command-and-control infrastructure“ ist die feststehende Fachfügung.

items.q: The state ____ any involvement, dismissing the accusation as baseless.
items.e: „deny“ = bloßes Bestreiten; „refute/rebut“ implizieren eine Widerlegung mit Beweisen, was hier zu stark wäre.

items.q: Forensic teams matched the intrusion's ____ to a group tracked for over a decade.
items.e: „tradecraft“ ist der spezifische geheimdienstliche Fachbegriff für charakteristische Vorgehensweisen.

items.q: Investigators uncovered a hidden ____ door left by the attackers for future access.
items.e: „backdoor“ = Hintertür, feststehender IT-Sicherheits-Fachbegriff.

items.q: The ministry's incident-response team moved swiftly to ____ the breach before it spread further.
items.e: „contain a breach“ = eindämmen; die anderen Verben kollokieren nicht mit „breach“.

items.q: The leaked cables were later confirmed to be ____ , not fabricated.
items.e: „confirmed to be authentic“ ist die im diplomatischen Register erwartete Formulierung.

items.q: The group's ____ suggests years of state sponsorship rather than criminal opportunism.
items.e: „sophistication“ ist der Standardbegriff der IT-Sicherheit für das technische Niveau eines Angriffs.

items.q: Analysts warned against ____ attribution, where isolated technical clues are stretched into sweeping political conclusions.
items.e: „premature attribution“ ist ein etablierter Begriff im Cyber-Sicherheitsdiskurs.

items.q: The state's ____ denial did little to dispel suspicion given the mounting technical evidence.
items.e: „blanket denial“ ist die feste idiomatische Wendung.

items.q: The breach exposed a treasure ____ of classified diplomatic correspondence.
items.e: „treasure trove“ ist die feste, hier übertragen gebrauchte Redewendung.

items.q: The victim state opted to ____ the accusation publicly rather than respond through quiet diplomatic channels.
items.e: Idiom „to level an accusation at someone“.

items.q: The two agencies' assessments ____ closely, lending the joint statement additional weight.
items.e: „converge“ passt am besten zum Bild zusammenlaufender Einschätzungen.

items.q: The indictment named four officers of the state's military ____ unit.
items.e: „military intelligence unit“ ist die standardmäßige offizielle Bezeichnung.

items.q: The malware exploited a coding ____ that vendors had not yet identified.
items.e: „coding flaw“ ist die im Kontext passende Standardkollokation.

items.q: The group's digital ____ bore the unmistakable mark of a well-resourced state sponsor rather than a lone hacker.
items.e: Idiom „bear the mark of someone's handiwork“ = einer Person/Gruppe zugeschrieben werden können.

items.q: The government imposed targeted sanctions in direct ____ to the confirmed cyber-attack.
items.e: „response to“ ist im formellen diplomatischen Register die Standardkollokation.

items.q: The report's authors were careful to ____ their confidence level, rating the attribution as 'high' rather than 'certain'.

items.q: What is the main idea the author develops across the passage?
o: International law regulating private military and security firms has kept perfect pace with the industry's growth.
Existing legal instruments have failed to close a structural accountability gap as the industry has expanded far beyond its original role.
The Montreux Document created a powerful new international enforcement mechanism.
Only host states bear any responsibility for contractor abuses.
items.e: Kernthese: das Regelwerk „has barely moved“, während die Branche sich massiv ausgeweitet hat; keines der beiden zentralen Instrumente schließt die Rechenschaftslücke.
items.passage:
The private military and security industry has expanded from a niche wartime expedient into a permanent fixture of contemporary conflict, and international law has struggled, visibly, to keep pace. Firms that once merely guarded embassies and shipping lanes now train foreign armies, operate surveillance platforms and, in a handful of well-documented cases, fight directly alongside state forces while remaining formally outside any national chain of command. The legal architecture governing them, by contrast, has barely moved since the mercenary scandals of the 1960s that first prompted states to legislate.

Two instruments dominate the field, and both fall conspicuously short of a binding global regime. The Montreux Document, agreed in 2008, restates existing obligations under international humanitarian law and catalogues good practices, but binds only the states that choose to endorse it and creates no new enforcement mechanism whatsoever. The International Code of Conduct, a voluntary industry initiative, relies on self-certification and client pressure rather than judicial sanction. Neither instrument answers the question that most troubles human-rights lawyers: when a contractor's employee commits an abuse abroad, which state, if any, is obliged to prosecute?

That accountability gap is not merely theoretical. Home states are frequently reluctant to investigate nationals operating under foreign contracts, citing evidentiary difficulty or diplomatic sensitivity; host states, often the weaker party to the contracting relationship, may lack the capacity or the political will to do so; and the contracting states themselves, having outsourced the function precisely to limit their own exposure, have every incentive to look the other way. The contractor thus operates, functionally, in a legal grey space that no single instrument was designed to close.

Proposals for a binding treaty have circulated at the UN Human Rights Council for over a decade, championed chiefly by states wary of Western contractors and resisted, with equal consistency, by the states whose firms dominate the market. Given that stalemate, the more plausible path to reform runs not through Geneva but through contract law itself: states that write robust human-rights clauses, effective monitoring and clear liability provisions into their own procurement agreements can impose real discipline even absent a treaty. Whether enough of them will bother to do so remains, for now, an open question.
items.src: Übungstext im Stil von Foreign Affairs / The Economist (nicht offiziell)

items.q: According to the passage, what do private security firms now do beyond guarding embassies and shipping lanes?
o: They train foreign armies, operate surveillance platforms, and in some documented cases fight alongside state forces outside any national chain of command.
They exclusively provide unarmed consulting services to governments.
They have been formally absorbed into national armed forces everywhere.
They no longer operate in active conflict zones at all.
items.e: „now train foreign armies, operate surveillance platforms and... fight directly alongside state forces while remaining formally outside any national chain of command.“

items.q: What limitation does the passage identify in both the Montreux Document and the International Code of Conduct?
o: Both are legally binding on every state in the world.
Neither creates a judicial enforcement mechanism that firms cannot avoid.
Both were drafted exclusively by private security firms themselves.
Both have been formally abolished by the UN Human Rights Council.
items.e: Montreux „creates no new enforcement mechanism whatsoever“; der Kodex „relies on self-certification and client pressure rather than judicial sanction.“

items.q: What can be inferred about contracting states' incentives regarding investigation of contractor abuses?
o: They have every incentive to investigate thoroughly, since abuses damage their own reputation directly.
Having outsourced the function to limit their own exposure, they have an incentive to avoid scrutiny.
They are legally barred from investigating any contractor under international law.
They delegate all investigative authority to the firms themselves by treaty.
items.e: „the contracting states themselves, having outsourced the function precisely to limit their own exposure, have every incentive to look the other way.“

items.q: In context, 'a legal grey space' most nearly describes a situation in which a contractor …
o: is subject to overlapping, excessively strict jurisdictions.
falls outside any jurisdiction willing or able to hold it accountable.
is granted full diplomatic immunity by treaty.
items.e: „grey space“ (wie „grey zone“) bezeichnet einen unklar geregelten Bereich — keine der drei beteiligten Staatengruppen übernimmt tatsächlich Verantwortung.

items.q: The author's tone throughout the passage is best described as …
o: uncritically supportive of the private security industry.
analytically critical, identifying structural gaps without dismissing the industry's function outright.
alarmist, predicting the imminent collapse of international law.
items.e: Sachlich-kritischer Ton: der Autor erkennt die Ausweitung der Branche an, kritisiert aber konsequent die fehlende Rechenschaftspflicht, ohne polemisch zu werden.

items.q: What is the primary function of the third paragraph, beginning 'That accountability gap is not merely theoretical'?
o: To prove that host states are solely responsible for all contractor abuses.
To explain, in turn, why none of the three categories of state involved has a strong incentive to pursue accountability.
To announce that the accountability gap has already been fully resolved.
To argue that home states always successfully prosecute abuses committed abroad.
items.e: Der Absatz erläutert nacheinander, warum Heimat-, Gast- und Auftragsstaat jeweils aus unterschiedlichen Gründen zurückhaltend bleiben.

items.q: According to the final paragraph, what does the author suggest as the more realistic path to reform, given the stalemate over a binding treaty?
o: Abandoning any attempt at regulation altogether.
Relying on individual states to embed robust human-rights and liability provisions directly into their own procurement contracts.
Waiting for the UN Human Rights Council to reach unanimous agreement.
Transferring all regulatory authority to the firms themselves.
items.e: „the more plausible path to reform runs not through Geneva but through contract law itself: states that write robust human-rights clauses, effective monitoring and clear liability provisions into their own procurement agreements can impose real discipline even absent a treaty.“

items.q: The scandal renewed international debate over how to regulate private military and security ____ operating in conflict zones.
items.e: „contractor“ ist der etablierte Fachbegriff für private Militär- und Sicherheitsfirmen und deren Personal.

items.q: Investigators struggled to determine which state was legally ____ to prosecute the abuse committed abroad.
items.e: „legally competent“ ist der präzise völkerrechtliche Fachbegriff für „zuständig“; „entitled“ und „authorised“ beschreiben eine andere Art von Befugnis.

items.q: Home states have often been reluctant to ____ nationals accused of abuses committed under foreign contracts.
items.e: „prosecute“ = strafrechtlich verfolgen; „persecute“ (verfolgen im Sinne von schikanieren) ist der klassische False-Friend-Fallstrick.

items.q: Governments increasingly ____ security functions once performed exclusively by national armed forces.
items.e: „outsource“ ist der Standardbegriff für die Auslagerung staatlicher Funktionen an private Anbieter; „relegate“ (herabstufen) passt inhaltlich nicht.

items.q: The contract left the question of legal ____ for battlefield conduct deliberately vague.
items.e: „liability“ ist der präzise rechtliche Fachbegriff für Haftung; die übrigen Substantive sind sinnverwandt, aber im vertragsrechtlichen Kontext weniger exakt.

items.q: Legal experts warn that unregulated contractors can end up operating in a jurisdictional ____ , answerable to no state in particular.
items.e: „no-man's-land“ (wörtl. Niemandsland) wird hier übertragen für einen rechtlich unregulierten Zwischenraum verwendet — die im Diskurs übliche bildhafte Wendung.

items.q: The council debated a binding legal ____ that would impose uniform accountability standards on the industry.
items.e: „legal instrument“ ist der Sammelbegriff für völkerrechtliche Verträge, Kodizes und ähnliche Regelwerke.

items.q: Firms operating abroad increasingly rely on ____ to reassure clients without inviting binding external oversight.
items.e: „self-certification“ bezeichnet konkret das eigenständige Bestätigen der Einhaltung von Standards ohne externe Prüfung; „self-regulation“ ist breiter gefasst.

items.q: The code of conduct is entirely ____ , and firms face no legal penalty for ignoring it.
items.e: „voluntary code“ ist die feste Fachfügung; die übrigen Adjektive sind sinnverwandt, aber keine etablierte Kollokation mit „code“.

items.q: Vetting new recruits thoroughly is meant to prevent individuals with a record of ____ from being deployed again.
items.e: „a record of misconduct“ ist die im Personalkontext übliche Standardkollokation.

items.q: Host governments frequently lack the ____ to investigate abuses committed by foreign contractors on their own soil.
items.e: „lack the capacity to“ ist die im sicherheitspolitischen Register etablierte Standardkollokation.

items.q: Talks on a binding treaty have reached a ____ at the UN Human Rights Council for over a decade.
items.e: „reach a deadlock“ = sich festfahren; im UN-Kontext die gebräuchliche Formulierung für blockierte Verhandlungen.

items.q: The firm's contract with the ministry included a robust human-rights ____ obliging it to report any abuse.
items.e: „human-rights clause“ ist die etablierte Fachfügung in Beschaffungs- und Handelsverträgen.

items.q: Without an effective ____ mechanism, even the best-written contract clauses remain unenforced in practice.
items.e: „monitoring mechanism“ ist die feste Fachfügung; die übrigen Gerundien bilden keine etablierten Komposita mit „mechanism“.

items.q: The state's licensing ____ requires firms to renew their authorisation to operate abroad every two years.
items.e: „licensing framework“ ist die im Regulierungskontext gebräuchliche Fachfügung.

items.q: Analysts warn that without external oversight, the industry risks operating with near-total ____ .
items.e: „impunity“ = faktische Straflosigkeit (ein Zustand); „immunity“ bezeichnet eine formal verliehene rechtliche Immunität — der entscheidende Bedeutungsunterschied.

items.q: The report accused several firms of operating with insufficient regard for their employees' ____ status under humanitarian law.
items.e: „combatant status“ ist der präzise humanitärrechtliche Fachbegriff (Genfer Konventionen).

items.q: Contractors who take a direct part in hostilities may forfeit any claim to civilian ____ under the law of armed conflict.
items.e: „civilian immunity“ ist der humanitärrechtliche Fachbegriff für den Schutzstatus von Zivilpersonen.

items.q: The UN working group's mandate is to ____ allegations of human-rights abuses linked to the industry.
items.e: „investigate allegations“ ist die im Menschenrechtskontext übliche Standardkollokation.

items.q: Weak parliamentary ____ has allowed several governments to sign contractor agreements with little public scrutiny.
items.e: „parliamentary oversight“ ist die feste politikwissenschaftliche Fachfügung; „surveillance“ trägt eine andere, eher nachrichtendienstliche Konnotation.

items.q: Two mercenary conventions from the 1970s and 1980s have been widely criticised as ____ , ratified by too few states to matter.
items.e: „toothless“ (wörtl. zahnlos) = wirkungslos, ohne Durchsetzungskraft; etablierte Metapher für Regelwerke ohne Sanktionsmechanismus.

items.q: The firm's board dismissed the allegations as an attempt to ____ its reputation ahead of a major government tender.
items.e: „tarnish a reputation“ ist die gebräuchlichste Kollokation.

items.q: „Rechenschaftspflicht“ — das exakte englische Äquivalent:
items.e: „accountability“ ist der etablierte politik-/verwaltungswissenschaftliche Fachbegriff für Rechenschaftspflicht.

items.q: „Verhaltenskodex“ — das exakte englische Äquivalent:
items.e: „code of conduct“ ist der etablierte Fachbegriff, wie im Text mit dem „International Code of Conduct“ belegt.

items.q: „nichtstaatlicher Akteur“ — das exakte Äquivalent:
items.e: „non-state actor“ ist der etablierte völkerrechtliche Fachbegriff.

items.q: „Vergabeverfahren“ (öffentliche Aufträge) — das exakte Äquivalent:
items.e: „tendering procedure“ ist der etablierte Fachbegriff für das Vergabeverfahren bei öffentlichen Aufträgen.

items.q: The court demanded that the contractor ____ full records of the incident before ruling on the case.
items.e: Mandativer Subjunktiv nach „demand that“ — Grundform ohne -s.

items.q: Had the ministry vetted the firm more rigorously, the abuse ____ entirely preventable in hindsight.
items.e: Gemischter Konditional: Bedingung Vergangenheit, Folge Gegenwart.

items.q: ____ the firm to lose its licence, thousands of contracts would have to be renegotiated overnight.
items.e: „Were … to“ — invertierte hypothetische Zukunftsform.

items.q: No sooner had the contract been signed ____ reports of abuse began to surface.
items.e: Feste Korrelation „no sooner … than“.

items.q: The abuse ____ have gone unnoticed at headquarters; incident reports were filed with the London office every week.
items.e: „can't have“ = logische Unmöglichkeit im Rückblick.

items.q: The oversight committee ____ its annual report only last Friday.
items.e: Abgeschlossener Zeitpunkt („last Friday“) schließt das Present Perfect aus.

items.q: By the time the inquiry concludes, the firm ____ in the country for over a decade.
items.e: Future Perfect nach „by the time“ bei andauernder Handlung.

items.q: A number of contractors ____ still under investigation for the incident.
items.e: „a number of“ + Plural.

items.q: The longer the inquiry dragged on, ____ the firm's public reputation became.
items.e: Korrelative Struktur „the … the …“ verlangt zwei Artikel.

items.q: The board withheld the internal review ____ it invite further litigation.
items.e: „lest“ + Subjunktiv (Grundform).

items.q: ____ troubled investigators most was not the incident itself but the firm's attempt to conceal it.
items.e: Pseudo-Cleft „What … was …“.

items.q: The board reviewed the allegations and ____ within a week.
items.e: Pronominales Objekt steht zwingend zwischen Verb und Partikel.

items.q: The unit is believed ____ unauthorised weapons across the border months before the incident.
items.e: Berichtspassiv mit Vorzeitigkeit: „is believed to have smuggled“.

items.q: Having outlined the allegations, the investigator went on ____ several policy recommendations.
items.e: „go on to do“ = zu einer neuen Handlung übergehen.

items.q: The ministry would rather the contract ____ quietly rather than through public litigation.
items.e: „would rather“ + Simple Past bei Gegenwarts-/Zukunftsbezug; „had ended“ wäre nur bei Vergangenheitsbezug korrekt.

items.q: The provision ____ the ministry objected has since been struck from the final contract.
items.e: Vorangestellte Präposition verlangt „which“, nie „that“.

items.q: ____ hastily after the scandal broke, the new licensing rules left several loopholes unaddressed.
items.e: Passivisches Partizip; die Aktivformen machten die Regeln zum Verfasser.

items.q: The firm's account of the incident was ____ inconsistent with witness testimony.
items.e: Adverb modifiziert das Adjektiv „inconsistent“.

items.q: The spokesperson had promised a full internal review ____ ; it never materialised.
items.e: Deixisverschiebung in der Redewiedergabe: „next month“ → „the following month“.

items.q: ____ did the report confirm the abuse, but it also named the officers responsible.
items.e: „Not only … but also“ verlangt Inversion nach vorangestelltem „Not only“.

items.q: Hardly had the ministry issued its denial ____ leaked documents contradicted it.
items.e: „hardly … when“ (im Unterschied zu „no sooner … than“).

items.q: The spokesperson briefed reporters as though the investigation ____ already concluded.
items.e: „as though“ + Past Perfect bei Bezug auf eine vorzeitige, irreale Situation.

items.q: The response team ____ have suspended every contract; only one unit was implicated in the abuse.
items.e: „needn't have + Partizip“ = unnötige, aber tatsächlich ausgeführte Handlung.

items.q: She was appointed ____ independent monitor for the region's private security sector last year.
items.e: Nullartikel vor einmaligen Ämtern nach „appoint“.

items.q: The leaked contract bears directly ____ the question of who authorised the operation.
items.e: „bear on“ = betreffen.

items.q: It is essential that every contractor ____ fully with the tribunal's investigation.
items.e: Mandativer Subjunktiv nach „it is essential that“.

Jede Frage 1 Punkt, insgesamt 60 Punkte, bestanden ab 30 Punkten (50 %). Trainingsniveau C2 – offizielles Prüfungsniveau C1+. Nicht offiziell.

items.q: What is the principal thesis advanced in the passage?
o: The veto has been formally abolished at the General Assembly's request.
Reform is blocked less by lack of consensus on substance than by the veto-holders' unwillingness to cede leverage.
African states have already secured a permanent seat on the Council.
The war in Ukraine has resolved the decades-old reform debate.
items.e: Der Text betont, dass die Blockade primär an der Veto-Arithmetik liegt, nicht am Mangel an Reformvorschlägen. Beleg: „Any amendment to the Charter requires ratification... precisely the states least inclined to dilute a privilege they alone possess.“
items.passage:
The clamour for a reformed Security Council is almost as old as the Council itself, yet it has rarely sounded so insistent as it does today. Aspirant powers — India, Brazil, Germany, Japan among them — argue with some justice that a body frozen in the geometry of 1945 can no longer claim to speak for a world it barely resembles. Africa, notably, remains without a single permanent seat, an omission that successive secretaries-general have called indefensible without ever quite saying so in public.

Yet reform proposals founder, as they have for three decades, on the awkward arithmetic of the veto. Any amendment to the Charter requires ratification by two-thirds of the General Assembly, including all five permanent members — precisely the states least inclined to dilute a privilege they alone possess. Model A, favoured by the G4 grouping, would add new permanent seats; Model B, championed by the self-styled Uniting for Consensus caucus, would instead multiply longer-term, renewable non-permanent seats, sidestepping the veto question altogether. Neither has come close to commanding the requisite majority.

What distinguishes the current push from earlier, equally earnest attempts is less its substance than its timing. The war in Ukraine, prosecuted by a permanent member against a UN member state, has lent the reform debate an urgency that abstract appeals to representativeness never quite achieved. Even so, sceptics note that the five incumbents have shown no discernible appetite for surrendering leverage merely because critics find its exercise embarrassing. The likeliest outcome, diplomats concede privately, is not wholesale restructuring but incremental adjustment: expanded consultation, sunset clauses on non-permanent terms, perhaps a voluntary code restraining veto use in cases of mass atrocity. Grand architecture may have to wait for a crisis graver than any yet endured — assuming, that is, the institution itself survives to be reformed.
items.src: Übungstext im Stil von Foreign Affairs / The Economist (nicht offiziell)

items.q: According to the passage, which region currently holds no permanent seat on the Security Council?
items.e: Laut Text: „Africa, notably, remains without a single permanent seat.“

items.q: What distinguishes Model B from Model A, as described in the passage?
o: Model B abolishes the veto outright, while Model A retains it.
Model B creates longer-term, renewable non-permanent seats instead of new permanent ones.
Model B is backed by the G4 grouping, while Model A is not.
Model B requires unanimous consent of the General Assembly.
items.e: Model B (Uniting for Consensus) setzt auf verlängerbare nichtständige Sitze statt neuer ständiger Sitze, um die Vetofrage zu umgehen.

items.q: What threshold does the passage say is required to amend the UN Charter?
o: A simple majority of the Security Council.
Two-thirds of the General Assembly, including all five permanent members.
Unanimous consent of all UN member states.
A referendum in each member state.
items.e: Text: „Any amendment to the Charter requires ratification by two-thirds of the General Assembly, including all five permanent members.“

items.q: What can be inferred about the five permanent members' likely response to sweeping reform proposals?
o: They will readily relinquish the veto once persuaded by moral argument.
They are likely to resist changes that would dilute their exclusive privilege.
They have already agreed to a binding timetable for reform.
They favour abolishing the General Assembly's ratification role.
items.e: Aus dem Kontext („the states least inclined to dilute a privilege they alone possess“, „shown no discernible appetite for surrendering leverage“) lässt sich ableiten, dass die P5 Widerstand leisten werden.

items.q: In the phrase 'reform proposals founder... on the awkward arithmetic of the veto', the word 'founder' most nearly means …
items.e: „founder“ (Verb) = scheitern/untergehen, nicht zu verwechseln mit „founder“ (Substantiv, Gründer).

items.q: The author's tone toward the prospects for sweeping Security Council reform is best described as …
items.e: Der Autor erkennt die Dringlichkeit an, bleibt aber skeptisch gegenüber tatsächlichem Wandel („The likeliest outcome... is not wholesale restructuring but incremental adjustment“).

items.q: The final paragraph is best described as performing which function?
o: To announce that reform has already been achieved.
To contrast the current sense of urgency with the P5's likely resistance and suggest a modest, incremental outcome.
To list all previous secretaries-general who supported reform.
To argue that the war in Ukraine is unrelated to the reform debate.
items.e: Der letzte Absatz stellt die neue Dringlichkeit dem wahrscheinlichen Ergebnis gegenüber: nicht Umbau, sondern kleine Anpassungen.

items.q: The five permanent members ____ over the wording of the resolution for nearly a week.
items.e: „to haggle over“ = feilschen/zäh verhandeln um Formulierungen.

items.q: The ambassador called for a ____ vote rather than a show of hands.
items.e: „a recorded vote“ = namentliche Abstimmung; feste Kollokation.

items.q: The G4 nations ____ their bid for permanent seats at the summit.
items.e: „renew a bid“ = ein Ansinnen erneuern; „renege“ = zurücktreten von einer Zusage, „rescind/revoke“ = widerrufen — falsche Bedeutung im Kontext.

items.q: Diplomats spent the recess trying to ____ a compromise text.
items.e: „to thrash out an agreement“ = eine Einigung mühsam aushandeln.

items.q: The Secretariat will ____ a revised draft ahead of the next session.
items.e: „to circulate a draft“ = einen Entwurf verteilen/zirkulieren lassen.

items.q: The reform initiative has gathered considerable ____ among mid-sized powers.
items.e: „to gather momentum“ = an Fahrt/Dynamik gewinnen.

items.q: Several delegations ____ reservations about the proposed seat allocation.
items.e: „to air reservations/concerns“ = Bedenken öffentlich äußern.

items.q: The proposal failed to secure the necessary ____ majority.
items.e: „a qualified majority“ = eine qualifizierte Mehrheit (fester EU-/UN-Terminus).

items.q: The chair called for a brief ____ to allow informal consultations.
items.e: „to call a recess“ = eine Sitzungspause einlegen.

items.q: The resolution was adopted ____ , without a single vote against.
items.e: „unanimously“ = einstimmig; „unilaterally“ = einseitig — häufige Verwechslung.

items.q: The delegation's position has remained largely ____ since the last round.

items.e: Pronominales Objekt steht zwingend zwischen Verb und Partikel.

items.q: What is the author's central contention about summit communiqués?
o: They are legally binding instruments that commit governments to specific budgets.
Their drafting is laborious and their language often deliberately vague, prompting debate over their real value.
They have replaced the need for heads of state to meet in person.
Sherpas are chosen at random from each ministry.
items.e: Kernaussage: mühsame Aushandlung, oft vage Sprache; Debatte über den tatsächlichen Nutzen (Signalwirkung vs. leere Rhetorik).
items.passage:
Few documents are laboured over so intensively, and read so cursorily, as the summit communiqué. Sherpas — the personal envoys who prepare the ground for heads of state and government — spend months haggling over paragraphs that most citizens will never open, let alone finish. Each clause is a small negotiation in itself: a single adjective softened or sharpened can signal, to those fluent in the genre, whether a coalition has actually agreed on substance or merely on language vague enough to paper over its divisions.

The ritual has grown more fraught as summits have swollen in size and ambition. What began, at the first G7 gatherings of the 1970s, as a handful of leaders conferring informally over economic coordination has become an unwieldy assembly of ministries, each insisting that its priority be reflected in the final text. Climate negotiators wrangle with trade officials over a single footnote; finance ministries resist commitments that might bind future budgets. By the time leaders arrive, the substantive work is largely done — their signatures affix a text that Sherpas have already fought to exhaustion over successive drafting rounds.

Critics contend that communiqués have become an exercise in diplomatic theatre, their length inversely proportional to their bite. A forty-paragraph statement studded with words like 'welcome', 'reaffirm' and 'encourage' can conceal as much as it reveals; commitments phrased in the conditional or hedged with 'as appropriate' bind no one to anything in particular. Defenders reply that the communiqué's real value lies not in enforceability but in signalling: it fixes, however loosely, a shared vocabulary that officials can invoke in subsequent negotiations. Whether that modest function justifies months of drafting brinkmanship is a question the participants rarely pause to ask themselves, absorbed as they are in the next comma.
items.src: Übungstext im Stil von Foreign Affairs / The Economist (nicht offiziell)

items.q: According to the passage, who are 'Sherpas'?
o: Heads of state attending the summit in person.
Personal envoys who prepare the ground ahead of the summit.
Officials responsible only for security arrangements.
items.e: Text: „Sherpas — the personal envoys who prepare the ground for heads of state and government“.

items.q: What does the passage say about the substantive work by the time leaders arrive?
o: It is largely complete, having been fought over in earlier drafting rounds.
It is postponed until after the summit.
It is decided solely by the host nation.
items.e: Text: „By the time leaders arrive, the substantive work is largely done.“

items.q: What example does the passage give of interministerial friction during drafting?
o: Defence ministries versus health ministries over troop deployments.
Climate negotiators wrangling with trade officials over a footnote.
Central banks refusing to attend meetings.
Sherpas refusing to draft any text at all.
items.e: Text: „Climate negotiators wrangle with trade officials over a single footnote.“

items.q: What can be inferred about phrases such as 'as appropriate' in communiqués?
o: They are inserted purely for stylistic elegance.
They are used to soften commitments so that no party is bound to a specific action.
items.e: Aus dem Kontext („bind no one to anything in particular“) folgt: solche Formulierungen dienen der Abschwächung von Verpflichtungen.

items.q: In 'their length inversely proportional to their bite', the word 'bite' most nearly means …
items.e: Übertragen: „bite“ = tatsächliche Durchschlagskraft/Wirkung eines Textes, nicht wörtlich.

items.q: The author's attitude toward the communiqué-drafting process is best described as …
o: wholly dismissive of any value it might have.
wryly critical, while acknowledging a modest defence of its purpose.
items.e: Der Text zitiert sowohl Kritiker als auch Verteidiger und schließt mit einer ironischen Schlussbemerkung („absorbed... in the next comma“) — kritisch-ironisch, nicht pauschal ablehnend.

items.q: How does the third paragraph relate the criticism of communiqués to their defenders?

To present both a critical view and a defence of the communiqué's purpose.
To announce the cancellation of future summits.
To describe the security protocol for heads of state.
items.e: Der Absatz stellt Kritiker („diplomatic theatre“) und Verteidiger („signalling“) gegenüber.

items.q: It was the finance ministry, not the foreign ministry, ____ blocked the paragraph.

items.q: The more paragraphs were added, ____ the statement became.
items.e: Korrelative Struktur „the … the …“; zweiter Artikel obligatorisch.

items.q: Hardly had the ink dried ____ a dissenting minister challenged the wording.

items.q: ____ overnight by exhausted officials, the final paragraph still contained an inconsistency.

items.q: What is the passage's central point about track-two diplomacy?
o: It always leads directly to a formal treaty within a year.
It allows unofficial actors to test ideas with a deniability that official negotiators cannot risk.
It has replaced formal diplomacy entirely.
It is illegal under international law.
items.e: Kernaussage: Track-Two erlaubt das Testen von Ideen durch informelle Akteure ohne offizielles Risiko, siehe „can therefore be disowned“.
items.passage:
Officially, nothing happened. No minister travelled, no statement was issued, and the two governments continued to trade the customary reproaches in public. Yet for eighteen months, retired generals, former ambassadors and academics from both countries had been meeting quietly in a succession of European capitals, testing formulas that neither foreign ministry could yet afford to propose out loud. This is track-two diplomacy: the practice of exploring settlement terms through participants who carry no official mandate and can therefore be disowned the moment a meeting becomes inconvenient.

Its appeal lies precisely in that deniability. A minister who floats a concession in public risks a domestic backlash he may never recover from; a retired diplomat who raises the same idea over dinner risks nothing more than being politely ignored. Ideas can be tested, refined or quietly buried without either capital committing itself. Sceptics counter that this very deniability is also the format's chief limitation: whatever is agreed around the table carries no binding force, and back-channel interlocutors, however well-connected, cannot deliver their governments' signatures.

The record is nonetheless instructive. The secret Oslo channel that produced the 1993 accords began as an academic seminar; contacts between American and Chinese intermediaries in the early 1970s likewise preceded, and made possible, the formal rapprochement that followed. What such episodes share is a narrow but real function: track-two talks do not replace formal negotiation, but they can identify, well before any official is willing to say so publicly, where common ground might plausibly exist. Whether the current round of quiet conversations will follow that pattern, or simply dissolve once the domestic political weather changes, remains, as ever with this kind of diplomacy, deliberately unknowable to all but the participants themselves.
items.src: Übungstext im Stil von Foreign Affairs / The Economist (nicht offiziell)

items.q: Who took part in the eighteen-month talks described at the start of the passage?
o: Retired generals, former ambassadors and academics.
items.e: Text: „retired generals, former ambassadors and academics from both countries“.

items.q: According to the passage, what historical example began as an academic seminar?
items.e: Text: „The secret Oslo channel that produced the 1993 accords began as an academic seminar.“

items.q: What do sceptics identify as the chief limitation of track-two diplomacy?
o: It is too expensive to organise.
Agreements reached carry no binding force and interlocutors cannot deliver their governments' signatures.
It always leaks to the press immediately.
It requires UN Security Council approval.
items.e: Text: „whatever is agreed around the table carries no binding force... cannot deliver their governments' signatures.“

items.q: What can be inferred about a minister who publicly floats a concession, compared with a retired diplomat who does the same privately?
o: The minister risks domestic backlash, while the retired diplomat risks comparatively little.
The retired diplomat faces greater legal liability.
Neither faces any risk at all.
items.e: Aus dem Vergleich im Text: „A minister... risks a domestic backlash... a retired diplomat... risks nothing more than being politely ignored.“

items.q: In 'can therefore be disowned the moment a meeting becomes inconvenient', the word 'disowned' most nearly means …
items.e: „to disown“ = eine Verbindung offiziell abstreiten/sich distanzieren.

items.q: The author's tone toward track-two diplomacy is best described as …
o: cautiously appreciative, noting both its function and its limits.
items.e: Der Text erkennt eine „narrow but real function“ an, benennt aber auch klar die Grenzen — verhalten anerkennend, nicht unkritisch.

items.q: What role do historical precedents play in the third paragraph's argument?
o: To argue that track-two diplomacy is a modern invention.
To cite historical precedents supporting the claim that such talks can precede formal rapprochement.
To criticise the Oslo Accords as a failure.
To describe the security arrangements of secret meetings.
items.e: Der Absatz belegt mit Beispielen (Oslo, US-China 1970er) die These, dass Track-Two formeller Annäherung vorausgehen kann.

items.q: The two sides communicated through a discreet ____ for nearly a year before any official contact took place.
items.e: „back channel“ = inoffizieller Kommunikationskanal.

items.q: The retired diplomat acted as an unofficial ____ between the two governments.
items.e: „go-between“ = Vermittler/Mittelsperson.

items.q: Both governments maintained ____ deniability throughout the secret talks.
items.e: „plausible deniability“ = glaubhafte Abstreitbarkeit, fester Terminus.

items.q: The academics involved had no official ____ to negotiate on behalf of their governments.
items.e: „official mandate“ = offizielles Verhandlungsmandat.

items.q: The two sides used the seminar as a ____ for testing settlement ideas.
items.e: „sounding board“ = Resonanzboden/Testumfeld für Ideen.

items.q: If the meeting became public, both governments were prepared to ____ any knowledge of it.
items.e: „to deny knowledge of something“ = jede Kenntnis abstreiten.

items.q: The channel allowed both sides to ____ ideas without formal commitment.
items.e: „to float an idea“ = eine Idee vorsichtig ins Spiel bringen.

items.q: The participants met under conditions of strict ____ .
items.e: „under conditions of confidentiality“ = unter strikter Vertraulichkeit.

items.q: Contacts of this kind often ____ the ground for formal negotiations later on.
items.e: „to prepare the ground“ = den Boden bereiten.

items.q: The intermediary carried no official ____ and could be repudiated at any time.
items.e: „official standing“ = offizieller Status/Stellung.

items.q: The two academics were quietly ____ by their respective foreign ministries to explore the idea.
items.e: „to be briefed by someone“ = informiert/instruiert werden.

items.q: The back-channel talks eventually ____ into a formal negotiating track.
items.e: „to evolve into something“ = sich zu etwas entwickeln.

items.q: The two envoys agreed to keep the discussions entirely ____ the record.
items.e: „off the record“ = nicht zur offiziellen Verwendung bestimmt.

items.q: The academic-turned-intermediary had ____ access to both foreign ministries.
items.e: „unrivalled access“ = unerreichter/einzigartiger Zugang.

items.q: The two delegations used a neutral venue to ____ suspicion.
items.e: „to allay suspicion“ = Verdacht zerstreuen; Homophon-Fallen: alloy/ally/alley.

items.q: The two governments' representatives met ____ the radar of the press for months.
items.e: „under the radar“ = unbemerkt, ohne öffentliche Aufmerksamkeit.

items.q: The unofficial talks were designed to ____ the way for an eventual summit.

items.q: What is the author's central point about ambassadorial recalls and PNG declarations?
o: They are purely symbolic and carry no diplomatic weight.
They are calibrated signals of serious displeasure that stop short of severing relations entirely.
They automatically trigger a declaration of war.
They are banned under the Vienna Convention.
items.e: Kernaussage: „calibrated: loud enough to register domestically, but rarely so final as to foreclose... quiet repair“.
items.passage:
Few gestures in diplomacy carry more calculated menace than the recall of an ambassador. It costs nothing in itself — no shot is fired, no treaty is torn up — yet it signals, in the starkest terms available short of severing relations altogether, that a government considers the relationship gravely, perhaps irreparably, strained. The declaration that an envoy is persona non grata, the formal expulsion that often accompanies such episodes, carries a similar weight: it tells the sending state, in language the Vienna Convention has made unmistakable, that its representative is no longer welcome and must leave within a stipulated period.

What makes these gestures useful to governments is precisely their reversibility. An ambassador withdrawn 'for consultations' can, in principle, return once tempers cool; a chargé d'affaires left in place ensures that some channel, however diminished, survives the rupture. Full-scale rupture of relations, by contrast, forecloses even that residual contact, which is why states reach for it far less readily than headlines might suggest. The theatre of recall, in other words, is calibrated: loud enough to register domestically, but rarely so final as to foreclose the possibility of quiet repair.

Tit-for-tat expulsions have become almost ritualised in certain rivalries, each side matching the other's number of departures with an exactness that suggests choreography rather than spontaneous outrage. Intelligence services often supply the pretext — an officer unmasked, a network rolled up — but the underlying message is rarely about espionage alone; it is about demonstrating that provocation will not go unanswered. Career diplomats caught in the crossfire tend to view the practice with weary resignation: postings can end within forty-eight hours, families uprooted mid-term, careers built and unbuilt by decisions made in ministries thousands of miles from where they actually serve.

items.q: What is the author's central point about treaty ratification?
o: Signature and ratification are legally identical acts.
Ratification procedures vary significantly by constitutional system and can derail treaties for reasons unrelated to their substance.
All democracies require a referendum to ratify treaties.
Ratification is always faster in presidential systems than in parliamentary ones.
items.e: Kernaussage: unterschiedliche Verfahren je nach Verfassungssystem, Scheitern oft aus sachfremden Gründen.
items.passage:
Signature and ratification are often conflated in casual speech, yet the distance between them can be measured in years, and occasionally in decades. A head of state's signature signals only that a government regards the negotiated text as acceptable; it creates, at most, an obligation not to defeat the treaty's object and purpose in the interim. Binding consent is a separate act, and constitutions differ sharply over who may grant it and under what conditions.

In presidential systems such as the United States, the executive negotiates but the legislature alone ratifies — and by a supermajority so demanding that entire treaty regimes, from the Law of the Sea Convention onward, have languished for decades awaiting a Senate vote that may never come. Parliamentary systems typically demand less: a simple majority in one or both chambers usually suffices, though federal states often add a further hurdle, requiring assent from constituent regions where the treaty touches on their competences. Some constitutions reserve a small category of especially sensitive agreements for direct popular ratification, submitting the text to a referendum before it can enter into force.

The consequences of this variation are not merely academic. A treaty painstakingly negotiated over years can collapse at the ratification stage for reasons having nothing to do with its substance — a change of government, an unrelated domestic scandal, or simple parliamentary indifference can each prove fatal. Negotiators have grown adept at anticipating these domestic veto points, sometimes shaping treaty language specifically to ease its passage through a particularly obstructive chamber. Whether this represents prudent statecraft or an unwelcome subordination of international commitments to domestic political weather is a question that divides practitioners as sharply as it divides academic opinion — and one unlikely to be settled so long as ratification remains, as the constitutions of most states insist it must, an essentially domestic affair.
items.src: Übungstext im Stil von Foreign Affairs / The Economist (nicht offiziell)

items.q: According to the passage, what is required to ratify a treaty in the U.S. system?
o: A simple majority in the House of Representatives.
A supermajority vote in the Senate.
Approval from all fifty state legislatures.
items.e: Text: „the legislature alone ratifies — and by a supermajority so demanding...“ (bezogen auf den Senat).

items.e: Text: „entire treaty regimes, from the Law of the Sea Convention onward, have languished for decades“.

items.q: What additional hurdle does the passage attribute to federal states?
o: A mandatory referendum for every treaty.
Requiring assent from constituent regions where the treaty touches their competences.
A requirement that the head of state personally travel abroad to sign.
A ban on ratifying trade treaties.
items.e: Text: „federal states often add a further hurdle, requiring assent from constituent regions where the treaty touches on their competences.“

items.q: What can be inferred about negotiators' behaviour, based on the third paragraph?
o: They ignore domestic ratification politics entirely.
They sometimes adapt treaty language in anticipation of domestic ratification obstacles.
They always prefer referendums over parliamentary approval.
They refuse to negotiate with federal states.
items.e: Text: „Negotiators have grown adept at anticipating these domestic veto points, sometimes shaping treaty language specifically to ease its passage.“

items.q: In 'entire treaty regimes... have languished for decades', the word 'languished' most nearly means …
items.e: „to languish“ = ungenutzt/vernachlässigt verharren, nicht vorankommen.

items.q: The author's tone in the final paragraph is best described as …
o: dismissive of the entire ratification debate.
balanced, presenting the tension between two views without fully endorsing either.
strongly in favour of abolishing domestic ratification.
items.e: Der letzte Absatz stellt zwei Sichtweisen gegenüber („prudent statecraft or an unwelcome subordination“), ohne eindeutig Partei zu ergreifen.

items.q: What is the primary function of the second paragraph?
o: To argue that referendums are always superior to parliamentary ratification.
To compare how different constitutional systems structure the ratification process.
To describe the history of the Law of the Sea Convention in detail.
To criticise the United States Senate specifically.
items.e: Der Absatz vergleicht präsidentielle, parlamentarische, föderale und plebiszitäre Ratifikationsverfahren.

items.q: If the federal chambers ____ more cooperative, the treaty would already have been ratified.
items.e: Gemischter Konditional (Gegenwarts-Irrealis in der Bedingung).

items.e: Deixisverschiebung in der Redewiedergabe.

items.e: Inversion nach vorangestelltem „Not only“ im Präsens: „does“ vor dem Subjekt.

items.q: ____ by three successive parliaments, the treaty finally entered into force last spring.

items.q: ____ the implementing legislation, the committee moved swiftly to schedule the vote.

items.e: Nullartikel vor einmaligen Ämtern nach „elect“.

items.q: The upper chamber's approval remains conditional ____ regional consent.
items.e: Feste Rektion: „conditional on“.

items.q: The treaty's ratification is inseparable ____ the domestic political calendar.
items.e: Feste Rektion: „inseparable from“.

items.e: Pronominales Objekt zwingend zwischen Verb und Partikel: „put forward“.
